article_units.name: Britain: Health and the People
article_units.subtitle: A thousand years of medicine, surgery and public health from medieval Britain to the NHS.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Thematic study across all three eras, factors driving change in health and medicine

lessons.title: Medieval Medicine: Humours, Galen and the Doctor's World
lessons.description: How Galenic theory and the four humours shaped diagnosis and training in medieval Britain c1000-1500.
lessons.spec_anchor: Medieval medicine: approaches including natural, supernatural, ideas of Hippocratic and Galenic methods and treatments; the medieval doctor; training, beliefs about cause of illness.
key_content: Hippocratic clinical observation and the Hippocratic Corpus
Galen's four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) and the theory of opposites
Natural vs supernatural explanations of disease (miasma, sin, astrology, imbalance)
Training of medieval doctors at Salerno, Bologna, Oxford — book-learning over dissection
Diagnosis: urine charts, pulse, zodiac man, humoural matching
Why Galen survived: fit with Christian view of the divinely-ordered body, taught from Latin texts, no rival framework
lessons.exam_skill_focus: Describing the medieval doctor's worldview accurately for 8-mark significance and development questions on later figures who challenged it.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That medieval doctors were 'stupid' — they were operating coherently within a framework where humoural balance made sense; the issue was the framework itself was wrong, not their reasoning.

lessons.title: The Church, the Monastery and Islamic Medicine
lessons.description: How Christianity and Islam between them preserved, spread and shaped medieval medical practice.
lessons.spec_anchor: Medical progress: the contribution of Christianity to medical progress and treatment; hospitals; the nature and importance of Islamic medicine and surgery; surgery in medieval times, ideas and techniques.
key_content: Monastic infirmaries — clean water, herb gardens, structured care; St Bartholomew's 1123, St Thomas's 1173
The Church as both engine (literacy, preserving texts, charitable hospitals) and brake (banning dissection 1163, framing disease as sin)
Islamic Golden Age: Bimaristans, Al-Razi distinguishing smallpox from measles, Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine
Surgery in medieval times: cauterisation, trepanning, bonesetting, John of Arderne's fistula treatment, anaesthetic 'dwale'
How Islamic medicine returned to Europe via Toledo and Salerno translations
lessons.exam_skill_focus: Religion as a factor that pushed both ways — strong material for the 16-mark factor essay when 'superstition and religion' is the named factor.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That the Church only held medicine back. It also funded hospitals, preserved texts and produced trained practitioners; without monastic copying, Galen would have been lost.

lessons.title: Public Health in the Middle Ages and the Black Death
lessons.description: Towns, monasteries and the catastrophe of 1348 — beliefs, treatments and the limits of medieval public health.
lessons.spec_anchor: Public health in the Middle Ages: towns and monasteries; the Black Death in Britain, beliefs about its causes, treatment and prevention.
key_content: Public health in medieval towns — cesspits, rakers, butchery rules; vs monastic plumbing and reredorters
The Black Death arrives in Britain 1348 — bubonic and pneumonic plague
Beliefs about cause: God's punishment, miasma, planetary alignment, Jews (in Europe), foreigners
Treatments: prayer, processions, flagellation, herbal remedies, bleeding, posies of flowers
Prevention: quarantine in some towns, 1348 Royal proclamation cleaning London streets, fleeing the city
Aftermath: depopulation, Statute of Labourers 1351, Peasants' Revolt 1381, gradual change to wages and land
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark 'Explain a Development' question on the response to the Black Death — causal chain not narrative.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That medieval people did nothing — quarantine, cleaning streets, isolating the sick all happened, just without an effective theoretical basis.

lessons.title: Renaissance Anatomy: Vesalius, Paré and the Challenge to Galen
lessons.description: How human dissection and battlefield surgery began to crack Galen's authority in the 16th century.
lessons.spec_anchor: The impact of the Renaissance on Britain: challenge to medical authority in anatomy, physiology and surgery; the work of Vesalius, Paré, William Harvey; opposition to change.
key_content: The Renaissance context: humanism, printing press, return to original Greek texts, Reformation weakens Church monopoly
Vesalius at Padua: De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543) — corrected over 200 of Galen's anatomical errors
Ambroise Paré on the battlefield (1530s-1590s) — replaced boiling oil with soothing salve (chance discovery), used ligatures instead of cauterisation
Why uptake was slow in Britain: Galen still taught at universities, English language editions of Vesalius rare, no immediate change in treatment
Opposition: Vesalius accused of heresy, Paré ridiculed by Paris faculty
Communication factor: printing press multiplied effect of new ideas
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark significance of Vesalius or Paré — must cover both 'at the time' (their direct corrections) and 'over time' (foundation for later anatomy and surgery).
lessons.misconception_to_address: That Vesalius 'changed medicine' — his book changed anatomical knowledge but routine treatment continued on Galenic lines for over a century.

lessons.title: Harvey, Sydenham and Disease Treatment c1600-1750
lessons.description: Circulation, observation and the slow modernisation of physic — quackery, plague and a new clinical method.
lessons.spec_anchor: Dealing with disease: traditional and new methods of treatments; quackery; methods of treating disease; plague; the growth of hospitals; changes to the training and status of surgeons and physicians; the work of John Hunter.
key_content: William Harvey, De Motu Cordis (1628) — proved the heart pumps blood in a circulation, overturned Galen on liver-as-source
Thomas Sydenham, the 'English Hippocrates' — clinical observation, classifying diseases (smallpox, scarlet fever, gout)
Quackery and patent medicines — Daffy's Elixir, James's Powder; how communication (newspapers) spread them
The Great Plague of London (1665) — quarantine, plague doctors, no theoretical advance on 1348
Voluntary hospitals 1700s — Westminster (1719), Guy's (1724), London (1740) — change in scale not yet in theory
John Hunter (late 18th c) — scientific surgery, dissection-based teaching, taught Jenner
Surgeons separate from barbers (1745); physicians still elite, surgeons still trade
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 4-mark 'Two Ways Similar or Different' between medieval and 18th-century hospitals or doctors.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That Harvey's circulation discovery transformed treatment — it took until 1818 (Blundell, first human-to-human transfusion) and beyond before circulation theory yielded clinical applications.

lessons.title: Jenner, Vaccination and the Limits of 18th-Century Prevention
lessons.description: How a country doctor's chance observation produced vaccination — and why it was fiercely opposed.
lessons.spec_anchor: Prevention of disease: inoculation; Edward Jenner, vaccination and opposition to change.
key_content: Inoculation (variolation) — imported from Turkey by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu c1721; risky but reduced smallpox mortality
Jenner's Gloucestershire observation: milkmaids who had cowpox did not catch smallpox
1796 experiment on James Phipps; published Inquiry 1798
Why this was different: empirical, theory-free — Jenner could not explain WHY it worked, which fed opposition
Opposition: variolators (commercial loss), clergy (transferring 'beast matter' to humans, satirised in Gillray's 1802 cartoon), some doctors
Government response: 1802 grant £10,000, 1807 grant £20,000; 1853 Vaccination Act made it compulsory; 1898 conscience clause after riots
Significance over time: Pasteur extended the principle in 1880s; smallpox eradicated 1980 (WHO)
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark significance of Jenner — at the time (saved thousands) and over time (template for later vaccines, government role in compulsory health).
lessons.misconception_to_address: That Jenner discovered germ theory. He did not — vaccination worked but its mechanism was a black box for over 60 years until Pasteur.

lessons.title: Pasteur, Koch and the Germ Theory Revolution
lessons.description: How germ theory replaced miasma — and how scepticism in Britain delayed practical change.
lessons.spec_anchor: The development of Germ Theory and its impact on the treatment of disease in Britain: the importance of Pasteur, Robert Koch and microbe hunting; Pasteur and vaccination; Paul Ehrlich and magic bullets; everyday medical treatments and remedies.
key_content: Miasma theory dominant up to mid-19th century — bad air causes disease
Pasteur 1861 Germ Theory of Disease — published after work on fermentation for the brewing industry
Koch's microbe hunting: anthrax 1876, staining technique, agar-jelly culture; TB 1882; cholera 1883
Pasteur extends his vaccine principle: chicken cholera 1879 (chance — old culture left over holiday), anthrax 1881, rabies 1885
Paul Ehrlich, Salvarsan 606 (1909) — first 'magic bullet' for syphilis; Prontosil (1932) for streptococcal infection
British scepticism: many doctors trained on miasma; germ theory only filtered into NHS-era textbooks slowly
Communication factor: Pasteur and Koch competed publicly, German-French scientific rivalry drove output
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 16-mark factor essay practice — was 'science and technology' the main factor in understanding disease? Pasteur and Koch as your central case.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That germ theory was instantly accepted. Many British surgeons and public health officials clung to miasma into the 1880s.

lessons.title: A Revolution in Surgery: Anaesthetics and Antiseptics
lessons.description: How chloroform and carbolic acid moved surgery from butchery to safety — and why opposition slowed the change.
lessons.spec_anchor: A revolution in surgery: anaesthetics, including Simpson and chloroform; antiseptics, including Lister and carbolic acid; surgical procedures; aseptic surgery.
key_content: Pre-anaesthetic surgery: speed (Liston amputating in 28 seconds), high mortality, restricted to crisis cases
Nitrous oxide (Davy 1799), ether (Morton, Boston 1846), chloroform (Simpson, Edinburgh 1847)
Opposition to chloroform: clergy citing Genesis 'in sorrow shalt thou bring forth'; surgeons fearing patients died from anaesthetic; resolved partly by Queen Victoria's use in 1853 for Prince Leopold
The 'Black Period' 1846-1865 — anaesthetics encouraged longer, deeper surgery but infection killed 50% of patients
Lister 1865 reads Pasteur, applies carbolic acid in Glasgow; publishes The Lancet 1867
Resistance to Lister: spray was unpleasant, surgeons could not see germs, results variable; takes until 1880s to win consensus
Aseptic surgery (sterile environment, rubber gloves Halsted 1894) replaces antiseptic by 1900
WWI as accelerator — blood transfusions, X-rays (Röntgen 1895), shrapnel surgery
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark 'Explain a Development' on the development of antiseptic surgery — clear causal chain (germ theory + Listers reading + carbolic acid + falling mortality + uptake).
lessons.misconception_to_address: That anaesthetics solved surgery. They actually made the infection problem worse before Lister solved it.

lessons.title: Public Health in the Industrial City: Snow, Chadwick and the Acts
lessons.description: Cholera, the Broad Street pump and the long road from the 1848 Act to the 1875 Act.
lessons.spec_anchor: Improvements in public health: public health problems in industrial Britain; cholera epidemics; the role of public health reformers; local and national government involvement in public health improvement, including the 1848 and 1875 Public Health Acts.
key_content: Industrial Britain: rapid urbanisation, back-to-backs, no sewers, Whig laissez-faire opposition to state action
Edwin Chadwick, Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population (1842) — argued bad housing caused poverty not the reverse
1848 Public Health Act — General Board of Health, but adoptive (towns chose to opt in) and limited
John Snow 1854 — Broad Street pump map; removed handle; convinced local officials but not the medical establishment
Joseph Bazalgette's London sewers 1865 — built in response to the 1858 'Great Stink', validated by 1866 cholera not reaching sewered districts
1875 Public Health Act (Disraeli, after 1867 working-class franchise) — compulsory, comprehensive; Artisans' Dwellings Act same year
Why the shift? Government factor combines with science (Snow), communication (Punch cartoons, Mayhew's London Labour), and chance (Great Stink forcing Parliament to act)
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 16-mark factor essay — was government the main factor in improving public health? Compare 1848 to 1875.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That the 1848 Act fixed public health. It barely worked because it was adoptive and short-lived; the 1875 Act, after wider voting rights and germ theory, was the real shift.

lessons.title: Nightingale, Hospitals and the Reform of Nursing
lessons.description: How war, statistics and a determined individual transformed Victorian hospitals and the nursing profession.
lessons.spec_anchor: Improvements in public health (cont.); changes to the training and status of surgeons and physicians (linked); growth of hospitals.
key_content: Pre-Crimean nursing: untrained, often drunk, low status (Dickens's Sairey Gamp)
Crimean War 1854-56: Nightingale and 38 nurses to Scutari; mortality fell from ~42% to ~2% in six months
Nightingale used statistics — pioneered the rose diagram (polar area chart) to convince Parliament
Notes on Nursing (1859) and Notes on Hospitals (1859); Nightingale Training School at St Thomas's 1860
Pavilion-plan hospitals — long wards, ventilation, separation by disease
Mary Seacole — Crimean nurse, refused by War Office, ran 'British Hotel' near front; recognition delayed until late 20th century
Linked spec content: status of surgeons and physicians, growth of hospitals — both shift towards professional, regulated bodies (1858 Medical Act)
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark significance of Nightingale — at the time (Crimean mortality, lobbying) and over time (professional nursing, hospital design legacy).
lessons.misconception_to_address: That Nightingale single-handedly invented nursing. Catholic nursing orders pre-existed her; her achievement was making secular nursing a respected profession in Britain.

lessons.title: From Booth and Rowntree to the Liberal Reforms 1900-1914
lessons.description: How poverty surveys, the Boer War and a Liberal landslide put the state into welfare for the first time.
lessons.spec_anchor: The importance of Booth, Rowntree, and the Boer War; the Liberal social reforms.
key_content: Charles Booth, Life and Labour of the People in London (1889-1903) — 30% of Londoners below the poverty line
Seebohm Rowntree, Poverty: A Study of Town Life (1901) — 28% of York similar; 'primary' (insufficient income) vs 'secondary' poverty
Boer War 1899-1902: 40% of recruits in industrial cities rejected as unfit; national efficiency panic
1906 Liberal landslide — Campbell-Bannerman, then Asquith; pressure from Lloyd George, Churchill (then Liberal), Beveridge (civil servant)
Reforms: Free school meals (1906), School medical inspections (1907), Old Age Pensions Act (1908, means-tested, over 70), Labour Exchanges (1909), People's Budget (1909, Lords crisis)
National Insurance Act 1911 — Part I health insurance for workers (4d worker, 3d employer, 2d state, 'ninepence for fourpence'), Part II unemployment insurance for select trades
Limits: contributory not universal; wives and children mostly excluded; opposition from BMA, Labour, friendly societies
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark 'Explain a Development' on the Liberal reforms — preconditions (Booth, Rowntree, Boer War), trigger (1906 election), response (Acts), consequences (basis for later welfare state).
lessons.misconception_to_address: That the Liberal reforms were the welfare state. They were a partial, contributory, work-tested step — universal welfare waited for Beveridge and Bevan.

lessons.title: Penicillin, Modern Surgery and the Wars
lessons.description: How chance, individuals and the demands of two world wars produced the antibiotic age and modern surgery.
lessons.spec_anchor: Modern treatment of disease: the development of the pharmaceutical industry; penicillin, its discovery by Fleming, its development; new diseases and treatments, antibiotic resistance; alternative treatments. The impact of war and technology on surgery: plastic surgery; blood transfusions; X-rays; transplant surgery; modern surgical methods, including lasers, radiation therapy and keyhole surgery.
key_content: Fleming 1928 — chance contamination of staphylococcus plate by Penicillium notatum; published 1929 but moved on
Florey and Chain at Oxford from 1939 — purified penicillin, mouse experiment 1940, first human patient 1941 (PC Albert Alexander, died when supply ran out)
WWII brought US mass-production from 1941 — by D-Day 1944, enough for all Allied wounded; Nobel Prize 1945
Plastic surgery: Harold Gillies WWI (Queen's Hospital Sidcup); Archibald McIndoe WWII Guinea Pig Club at East Grinstead
Blood transfusions: Landsteiner blood groups 1901; WWI storage advances; National Blood Transfusion Service 1946
X-rays: Röntgen 1895; rapid wartime adoption from 1914
Modern surgery: keyhole (laparoscopic) from 1980s; transplants — Christiaan Barnard heart 1967; lasers; radiotherapy
Antibiotic resistance: MRSA from 1960s; rising public health concern from 1990s
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 16-mark factor essay — was 'chance' the main factor in modern medicine? Fleming's mould plus Pasteur's chicken cholera plus Paré's salve as a sweep across periods.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That Fleming created penicillin as a working drug. He saw the effect; Florey and Chain made it a medicine; war forced mass production.

lessons.title: Beveridge, Bevan and the Birth of the NHS
lessons.description: How the 1942 Beveridge Report and a Labour government created universal healthcare in 1948 — and the fights to get there.
lessons.spec_anchor: Modern public health: the impact of two world wars on public health, poverty and housing; the Beveridge Report and the Welfare State; creation and development of the National Health Service; costs, choices and the issues of healthcare in the 21st century.
key_content: WWII context: evacuation exposed urban poverty to rural Britain; rationing improved working-class diet; Emergency Medical Service nationalised hospitals temporarily
Beveridge Report December 1942 — five 'giants on the road to reconstruction': want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness
300,000 copies sold; popular pressure made post-war welfare politically unavoidable
1945 Labour landslide — Attlee government, Bevan as Minister of Health
NHS Act 1946 passed; opposition from Conservatives in Parliament and the BMA in the medical press
BMA January 1948: 'so grossly at variance with the essential principles of our profession that it should be rejected absolutely'
Bevan's compromise: consultants kept private patients ('I stuffed their mouths with gold'); GPs ran their own practices as contractors not employees
5 July 1948 — NHS opens; free at point of use, funded by taxation; first universal system in the world
Other welfare state Acts 1944-48: Education Act 1944, Family Allowances 1945, National Insurance Act 1946, National Assistance Act 1948
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 16-mark factor essay practice — was war the main factor in creating the NHS? WWII context vs Beveridge as individual vs Labour government.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That the NHS was a national consensus. Bevan won by political calculation against active medical opposition; the deal had explicit costs (private practice survives inside the NHS).

lessons.title: Weighing the Factors: Continuity, Change and Progress c1000-Today
lessons.description: Synthesising the seven factors across a thousand years to write a top-band 16-mark factor essay.
lessons.spec_anchor: All four parts; explicit synthesis lesson on the seven factors and the rate, direction and meaning of change.
key_content: Mapping the seven factors against the four spec parts — which factor dominates in which period?

The 16-mark factor essay structure: introduction (define factor + judgement), factor paragraph (named factor with two periods of evidence), counter-factor paragraphs (at least two other factors), conclusion (substantiated overall judgement)

Worked example: 'Has government been the main factor in improving public health? Explain your answer with reference to government and other factors.' — 1348 (almost no government), 1848 (weak), 1875 (strong), 1948 (decisive); compare to science and individuals
Tackling the change-vs-progress problem: not all change is progress (loss of Roman public health); progress depends on whose perspective
Tackling rate of change: medieval slow, Renaissance start-stop, 19th-century acceleration, 20th-century rapid
21st-century issues: NHS funding, ageing population, antibiotic resistance, mental health, COVID-19 pandemic — students should be able to extend the story to today
Examiner red flags: writing in first person, listing factors without judgement, using only one period, vague figures (the AQA examiner reports flag this every series)
lessons.exam_skill_focus: Whole-paper rehearsal — 4-mark, 8-mark significance, 8-mark development and 16-mark factors essay all modelled in this lesson with the seven factors as the spine.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That the 16-mark question is about cramming all seven factors. It is about weighing the named factor against two or three carefully chosen others, with three examples across at least two periods, and reaching a substantiated overall judgement.

teaching_brief.what_this_unit_is: A thematic study tracking how medicine, surgery and public health changed in Britain across roughly 1,000 years — medieval (c1000-c1500), Renaissance and early modern (c1500-c1750), industrial and Victorian (c1750-c1900), and modern (c1900-present). The seven AQA factors (war, religion/superstition, chance, government, communication, science and technology, the role of the individual) thread through every period and underpin the 16-mark factor essay that dominates the paper.
teaching_brief.what_is_assessed_overall: Paper 2 Section A is 40 marks of the GCSE total. Within this option students answer a fixed sequence of question types: a 4-mark 'Two Ways Similar or Different' between two periods, an 8-mark 'Explain Significance' on a named individual or development, an 8-mark 'Explain a Development', and a 16-mark 'Factors Essay' that names one factor and asks students to weigh it against others. The factor essay carries 40% of the option's marks and is the single highest-leverage skill in the unit.
core_narratives_students_must_master: Continuity then collapse: Galenic-Hippocratic medicine and the four humours dominated medieval Britain and only began to crack in the Renaissance — Vesalius (1543), Paré (1530s-90s) and Harvey (1628) corrected Galen on anatomy, surgery and circulation but did not change everyday practice for over a century.

Religion as both engine and brake: monasteries spread literacy, hospitals and care; Islamic medicine preserved Galen and added new ideas (Al-Razi, Ibn Sina); the Church then prevented dissection and treated disease as divine punishment, slowing change. Religion is therefore a factor that pushes both ways across the sweep.

Two leaps in disease theory: Jenner's vaccination (1796) was empirical but theory-free — he could not explain why cowpox prevented smallpox. Pasteur's germ theory (1860s) and Koch's microbe-hunting (1870s-80s) gave Lister the basis for antiseptic surgery (1867) and finally toppled miasma theory.

Public health, from individual responsibility to state duty: cholera epidemics (1831, 1848, 1854), Snow's Broad Street pump (1854), Chadwick's 1842 report, and the 1848 and 1875 Public Health Acts trace the shift from laissez-faire to compulsory government action.

From Liberal reforms to NHS: Booth and Rowntree's poverty studies, Boer War recruitment shock, the 1906-11 Liberal reforms, two world wars, the 1942 Beveridge Report, and Bevan's NHS in 1948 — a single causal chain students must hold together.

Modern challenges: Fleming's penicillin (1928, mass-produced 1940s), DNA and genetic medicine, keyhole surgery, antibiotic resistance, an ageing population, mental health and the cost crisis of 21st-century healthcare.

common_misconceptions.topic: Medieval medicine was 'backward' with no progress
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume nothing useful happened in medicine between c1000 and c1500 because supernatural causes and bleeding patients look ridiculous to modern eyes.
common_misconceptions.correction: Within its own framework medieval medicine made real progress — Islamic hospitals in Baghdad and Damascus were better organised than European ones, Al-Razi distinguished smallpox from measles, Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was a teaching standard for 600 years, herbal remedies often had genuine pharmacological effects, and monastic infirmaries provided structured care. The Black Death exposed the limits of the system but did not stop the system functioning.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA examiner reports on Health and the People; Wellcome Collection Health and the medieval church

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write that Vesalius's Fabrica (1543) or Harvey's De Motu Cordis (1628) immediately transformed medical practice in Britain.
common_misconceptions.correction: Both corrected Galen on anatomy and physiology but the impact on actual treatment was minimal for at least a century — Galenic teaching dominated universities, and it took until the 19th century for circulation theory to feed into clinical care via blood transfusions. The lesson here is the gap between discovery and application.
common_misconceptions.source: Britannica articles on Vesalius and Harvey; AQA mark scheme commentary on significance questions

common_misconceptions.topic: Germ theory and antiseptics happened simultaneously
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students conflate Pasteur's discovery (germ theory, published 1861) with practical application (Lister's antiseptic surgery, 1867 onwards) and assume germs were universally accepted by the 1870s.
common_misconceptions.correction: Pasteur proved germs caused fermentation in the 1860s; Lister applied this to surgery from 1865 and published in The Lancet in 1867; many British surgeons rejected antiseptics until the 1880s because they could not see germs and found carbolic acid spray cumbersome. Koch's identification of specific bacteria (1876 anthrax, 1882 TB) is what finally settled the question.
common_misconceptions.source: Science Museum on Lister's antisepsis system; Britannica on germ theory

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat the NHS in 1948 as a feel-good consensus moment.
common_misconceptions.correction: The British Medical Association told members to refuse to participate in January 1948 — six months before launch — calling Bevan's plan 'so grossly at variance with the essential principles of our profession that it should be rejected absolutely by all practitioners.' Bevan compromised by letting consultants keep private patients and GPs run their own practices ('I stuffed their mouths with gold'). Without that, there would be no NHS.
common_misconceptions.source: The National Archives, The foundation of the NHS

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write that every change in medical history is progress, missing the spec's explicit prompt to ask 'whether change brought progress.'
common_misconceptions.correction: Some change was regression (the loss of Roman public health after c450), some was sideways (medieval Christian hospitals replaced classical ones with different functions), some was contested (anti-vaccination movement, 1853 Vaccination Act resistance, NHS-resistant BMA). 'Progress' implies a benchmark — students need to name whose perspective they are judging from.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA spec 8145 4.4.2; AQA examiner reports on factor essays

common_misconceptions.topic: Listing factors instead of weighing the named factor
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students answer the 16-mark question by writing one paragraph on each factor without ever returning to the named factor in the question.
common_misconceptions.correction: The mark scheme rewards complex sustained judgement on the stated factor relative to others — top-band answers compare directly ('government action mattered more than science here because...') and reach a substantiated overall judgement, not a list.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA mark scheme 8145/2A/A; AQA examiner reports

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat each period in isolation and cannot give examples 'across two time periods' as the 16-mark question requires.
common_misconceptions.correction: Examiner reports flag that strong answers move fluently between periods (e.g. comparing the role of government in 1348, 1848 and 1948) rather than writing four self-contained mini-essays.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA examiner reports on Paper 2 Section A factor essays

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 16-mark factor essay must use at least three examples drawn from at least two different time periods, and must keep returning to the named factor — not just listing all seven.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA mark scheme 8145/2A/A specimen and June 2022; AQA examiner commentary

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 8-mark significance question rewards both importance at the time and importance over time — answers that only describe the figure's contribution at the moment of discovery cap at the lower mark band.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA examiner reports on significance questions

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 4-mark 'Two Ways Similar or Different' question wants two distinct comparisons — students who write one comparison twice or list features without comparing lose half the marks.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA mark scheme 8145/2A/A

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Across the unit, named individuals (Vesalius, Harvey, Paré, Hunter, Jenner, Pasteur, Koch, Ehrlich, Simpson, Lister, Snow, Chadwick, Nightingale, Booth, Rowntree, Beveridge, Bevan, Fleming, Florey, Chain) are explicit spec content — vague gestures at 'a scientist' or 'a doctor' are penalised.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA spec 8145 section 3.4.4 AA Britain: Health and the people

teaching_brief.thematic_factors_anchor: Every lesson should explicitly tag which of the seven AQA factors are at work and how they interact. The final two lessons synthesise these factors across the whole sweep so students can weigh them in the 16-mark essay. Factors: war, superstition and religion, chance, government, communication, science and technology, the role of the individual.

skills_focus_per_question_type.4_marks_two_ways_similar_or_different: Compare two specific developments across periods (e.g. medieval and modern hospitals; Jenner's vaccination and modern vaccination programmes). Two distinct comparisons, one sentence each, with a concrete example for each.
skills_focus_per_question_type.8_marks_explain_significance: Pick one named individual or development. Cover both importance at the time (what changed because of them) and importance over time (their legacy across later periods). Two-paragraph structure with linking phrases.
skills_focus_per_question_type.8_marks_explain_a_development: Take a specific development (e.g. 'the development of antiseptic surgery') and explain how and why it occurred. Causal chain — preconditions, trigger, response, consequence — not narrative description.
skills_focus_per_question_type.16_marks_factors_essay: Named factor in the question, weighed against at least two others, with three examples drawn from at least two different periods, reaching a substantiated overall judgement on whether the named factor was the main driver.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Galen
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Theory of the four humours, anatomy and physiology — dominant in medieval Britain and only seriously challenged by Vesalius and Harvey.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Hippocrates
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Clinical observation, Hippocratic Corpus, ethical principle — foundational for medieval doctor's training.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Al-Razi (Rhazes) and Ibn Sina (Avicenna)
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Preserved and extended Galenic medicine; Al-Razi distinguished smallpox from measles; Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine taught for 600 years.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Andreas Vesalius
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: De Humani Corporis Fabrica — corrected Galen's anatomy through human dissection.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Ambroise Paré
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Replaced cauterisation with ligatures; battlefield surgery; soothing salves.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William Harvey
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: De Motu Cordis — circulation of the blood.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Thomas Sydenham
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: 'English Hippocrates' — clinical observation, classification of diseases.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: John Hunter
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Scientific surgery; teacher of Jenner; experimental method.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Edward Jenner
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Vaccination using cowpox to prevent smallpox; opposition from clergy and variolators.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Louis Pasteur
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Germ theory of disease; later vaccines for chicken cholera, anthrax, rabies.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert Koch
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Specific microbes — anthrax 1876, TB 1882, cholera 1883; staining and culture techniques.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Paul Ehrlich
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Salvarsan 606, the first 'magic bullet' for syphilis.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: James Simpson
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Chloroform anaesthetic; opposition from clergy and surgeons.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Joseph Lister
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Carbolic acid antiseptic surgery in Glasgow; published in The Lancet 1867; resistance from older surgeons.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: John Snow
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Broad Street pump map — proved cholera was waterborne; preceded germ theory.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Edwin Chadwick
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population — laid groundwork for 1848 Public Health Act.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Florence Nightingale
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Crimean War nursing; Notes on Nursing 1859; reformed hospital design and nursing as profession.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Charles Booth and Seebohm Rowntree
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Poverty studies in London (Booth) and York (Rowntree) — provided evidence base for Liberal reforms.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: David Lloyd George and the Liberal government
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Old age pensions 1908; National Insurance Act 1911 (sickness and unemployment).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William Beveridge
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Beveridge Report — 'five giants' (want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness); blueprint for the welfare state.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Aneurin Bevan
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Created the NHS as Minister of Health; faced down BMA opposition through compromise.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey, Ernst Chain
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Fleming's accidental discovery of penicillin (1928); Florey and Chain mass-produced it for WWII; chance plus science plus war.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: British Medical Association (BMA)
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Initially rejected NHS; deal struck so consultants kept private practice and GPs ran their own surgeries.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Christian Church and monasteries
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Built and ran hospitals; preserved classical texts; restricted dissection; framed disease as divine punishment.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Islamic scholars and Bimaristans
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Hospitals in Baghdad, Damascus, Cairo; pharmacology; surgical instruments; teaching texts that returned to Europe via Spain.

article_units.name: Britain: Power and the People
article_units.subtitle: From Magna Carta to modern protest: how citizens have shaped the British state.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Thematic study across all three eras, the changing relationship between citizen and state

lessons.title: The Citizen and the State: A Thematic Toolkit, c1170-Present
lessons.description: Meet the seven factors AQA wants you to track and the four question types you'll be marked on.
spec_bullets_covered: overview of the changing citizen-state relationship
the seven factors (war, religion, chance, government, communication, economy, ideas, individuals)
core_content: What 'thematic study' means and why we leap across centuries
Britain c1170: a feudal kingdom — kings rule by divine right, most people are serfs, no Parliament yet
Britain today: a parliamentary democracy with universal suffrage, a Human Rights Act and protest as a legal right
The seven factors AQA tests, with one example of each you'll meet later
The four question types — 4-mark similar/different, 8-mark significance, 8-mark development, 16-mark factors essay — and what each rewards
Why judgement against the named factor matters more than how many examples you list
key_individuals_groups: framing only — no individual focus this lesson
lessons.exam_focus: Worked walkthrough of one 4-mark and one 16-mark stem; what the bands actually want.
lessons.factor_thread: All seven introduced; this lesson is the index for the rest.

lessons.title: Magna Carta and the Limits of Kingship, 1215
lessons.description: Why the barons rebelled against King John, what Magna Carta actually said, and the gap between 1215 and the modern myth.
spec_bullets_covered: Constraints on kingship: the barons' dissatisfaction with King John's rule and its resolution; Magna Carta, its terms and its short and long-term impact
core_content: King John's failures: lost French lands (1204), heavy scutage taxation, quarrel with Pope Innocent III, defeat at Bouvines 1214
The baronial revolt and the role of Archbishop Stephen Langton in drafting terms
Runnymede, June 1215: what the 63 clauses actually contain (church freedom, no taxation without consent of council of barons, due process for 'free men', regulation of weights and measures)
Short-term: John repudiates the charter, Pope annuls it, civil war resumes — John dies in October 1216
Reissue 1216, 1217, 1225 under Henry III: how Magna Carta survived
Long-term mythology: how 17th- and 18th-century lawyers reinterpreted clause 39 ('no free man shall be imprisoned…') as a foundation of liberty
The misconception trap: Magna Carta was not democratic, did not apply to most of the population, and was not a 'people's charter'
lessons.exam_focus: 8-mark 'explain the significance of Magna Carta in the changing relationship between citizen and state' — short term vs long term.
lessons.factor_thread: Government (royal overreach), the role of the individual (Langton), war (Bouvines as trigger).

lessons.title: Simon de Montfort and the Birth of Parliament, 1258-1265
lessons.description: How a quarrel between Henry III and his barons accidentally produced the first Parliament with elected commoners.
spec_bullets_covered: The origins of parliament: issues between King Henry III and his barons; the role of Simon de Montfort; the Provisions of Oxford and the Parliament of 1265 and their short and long-term impact
core_content: Henry III's reign: Sicilian Business, foreign favourites, baronial grievance
The Provisions of Oxford 1258: a 15-member baronial council to oversee the king
Civil war and the Battle of Lewes 1264 — Henry III captured
Simon de Montfort's Parliament January 1265: knights of the shire and burgesses from towns summoned for the first time alongside barons and bishops
Why de Montfort summoned commoners: he needed broader support against royalist holdouts
The Battle of Evesham August 1265: de Montfort killed, his body mutilated; royalists win
Long-term: Edward I's 'Model Parliament' 1295 keeps the format; the two-chamber Parliament evolves
Significance over time: not democratic intent — power-politics need — but it set a precedent for representation
lessons.exam_focus: 8-mark 'explain the development of Parliament between 1215 and 1265' — show the link from Magna Carta to Montfort.
lessons.factor_thread: Role of the individual (de Montfort), government (constitutional crisis), war (Lewes/Evesham).

lessons.title: The Peasants' Revolt, 1381
lessons.description: How a poll tax, plague-era labour shortages and a young king's broken promises sparked the largest medieval English rising.
spec_bullets_covered: Medieval revolt and royal authority: the social, economic and political causes of the Peasants' Revolt; actions by rebels and government; impact of the Peasants' Revolt
core_content: Long-term causes: the Black Death (1348-49) cut the population by ~40%, raising peasant bargaining power; the Statute of Labourers 1351 tried to freeze wages
Mid-term causes: Hundred Years War costs, weak government under the boy-king Richard II
Short-term trigger: the third poll tax of 1381 — a flat tax of 4d on every adult, deeply regressive
Action: rising in Essex and Kent late May; Wat Tyler emerges as Kent leader; John Ball preaches 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?'
London June 1381: rebels burn the Savoy Palace, behead the Archbishop of Canterbury Simon Sudbury and Treasurer Robert Hales
Smithfield meeting: Tyler killed; 14-year-old Richard II rides out and tells rebels 'I will be your captain'
Government response: rebels disperse on royal promises; promises broken within weeks; ringleaders executed (Ball hanged July 1381)
Impact: poll tax abandoned; serfdom continues to decline organically; the rising shows ordinary people will resist royal authority
lessons.exam_focus: 16-mark factors essay practice: 'Has the role of the individual been the main factor in causing protest?' — Wat Tyler and John Ball as one example, weighed against the economy (Black Death, poll tax).
lessons.factor_thread: Economy (poll tax), chance (Black Death), role of the individual (Ball, Tyler), communication (sermons and traveling preachers).

lessons.title: The Pilgrimage of Grace, 1536
lessons.description: The largest peacetime revolt in English history — and the religious crisis behind it.
spec_bullets_covered: Popular uprisings against the Crown: the social, economic, religious and political causes of the Pilgrimage of Grace; the implications for royal authority; Henry VIII and his government's reaction and the impact of the uprising
core_content: Context: Henry VIII's break with Rome (Act of Supremacy 1534), Cromwell's visitations, dissolution of smaller monasteries from 1536
Causes — religious: monasteries were spiritual, social and economic centres in the north; their loss felt like a war on Catholic identity
Causes — economic: poor harvests, rents rising, fear of taxation on baptisms and burials
Causes — political: northern resentment at Cromwell and 'low-born' advisers replacing traditional nobility
Action: Lincolnshire Rising October 1536; main Pilgrimage led by lawyer Robert Aske rallies ~30,000 in Yorkshire under the banner of the Five Wounds of Christ
Royal response: Henry VIII has no army to match; the Duke of Norfolk negotiates a pardon and a promise to discuss grievances
The trap: a smaller post-truce rising (Bigod's revolt, 1537) gives Henry the excuse to renege; Aske and ~200 others executed
Impact: Reformation continues; northern political voice crushed; later rebellions (1549, 1569) frame themselves more cautiously
Compare to 1381: both used royal promises that were broken, both ended in executions
lessons.exam_focus: 4-mark 'two ways the Pilgrimage of Grace was similar to the Peasants' Revolt' — compare causes, actions and outcomes.
lessons.factor_thread: Religion (dominant), economy, government, the role of the individual (Aske).

lessons.title: The English Revolution: Civil War, Regicide and Republic, 1642-1660
lessons.description: How a quarrel over money and religion ended with a king on the scaffold and England as a republic.
spec_bullets_covered: Divine Right and parliamentary authority: the causes of the English Revolution; the New Model Army and the development of political radicalism during the Civil War era; the short and long-term impact of the English Revolution, including the significance of trial and execution of Charles I and Oliver Cromwell and the Commonwealth
core_content: Causes: Charles I's belief in Divine Right; eleven years' personal rule (1629-40); ship money; conflict with Scottish Covenanters; Long Parliament; Grand Remonstrance 1641; attempted arrest of the Five Members 1642
War: 1642-46 (First Civil War), Battle of Naseby 1645
The New Model Army (1645): Parliament's professional, disciplined, ideologically motivated army; promotion by merit not birth
Political radicalism: the Levellers and the Putney Debates 1647; the Agreement of the People; demands for manhood suffrage and religious liberty
Trial and execution of Charles I, January 1649: a king tried by his own subjects — 'a precedent that England, and indeed the world, has never forgotten'
The Commonwealth and Protectorate under Cromwell 1649-58: regicide, but not democracy — the Levellers are suppressed, the Rump Parliament dissolved, a Lord Protector ruling much like a king
Restoration 1660: Charles II returns, but Parliament is now permanently superior — divine right is broken in practice if not in theory
Long-term significance: established that kings can be removed; seeded democratic ideas later movements would draw on (Chartists explicitly cited the Levellers)
lessons.exam_focus: 8-mark 'explain the significance of the trial and execution of Charles I' — short term (republic) and long term (parliamentary supremacy).
lessons.factor_thread: Ideas (Divine Right vs parliamentary authority, Leveller democracy), religion, war, government.

lessons.title: The American Revolution and 'No Taxation Without Representation', 1763-1783
lessons.description: Why ideas born in 17th-century England exploded in 18th-century America — and bounced back to shape British reform.
spec_bullets_covered: Royal authority and the right to representation: the causes of the American Revolution including the relationship between the government and people; impact and significance of the American Revolution
core_content: Background: the Seven Years War (1756-63) leaves Britain financially exhausted and protecting an enlarged colonial empire
Stamp Act 1765: first direct tax on the colonies; sparks 'No taxation without representation' protest
Townshend Duties 1767, Boston Massacre 1770, Boston Tea Party 1773 — Coercive Acts 1774
Declaration of Independence 1776: Lockean ideas of natural rights, government by consent — explicitly invoking the same arguments used in the English Revolution
War 1775-83: French entry 1778 decisive; British defeat at Yorktown 1781; Treaty of Paris 1783
Impact on Britain: loss of 13 colonies discredits Lord North's government; reform movement at home (Wyvill's Yorkshire Association) revives demands for parliamentary reform
Long-term: American republic becomes a working laboratory of representative democracy that British radicals point to throughout the 19th century
Connecting the parts: from 1265 (representation in principle) to 1649 (Parliament can remove a king) to 1776 (people can remove a Parliament that misrepresents them)
lessons.exam_focus: 8-mark 'explain the development of the idea of representation between 1215 and 1783' — Magna Carta to American Revolution.
lessons.factor_thread: Ideas (representation, consent), the economy (war debt and taxation), government, communication (pamphlets, newspapers).

lessons.title: Peterloo, the Great Reform Act and Chartism, 1819-1858
lessons.description: How working-class demands for the vote met state violence — and how Parliament finally cracked open the franchise.
spec_bullets_covered: The extension of the franchise: radical protest; the Great Reform Act, causes and impact, including further reform; Chartism, causes, actions and impact
core_content: Post-Napoleonic Britain: economic distress, Corn Laws 1815, Six Acts 1819 repressing protest
Peterloo Massacre, August 1819: 60,000 gather at St Peter's Field, Manchester; Henry 'Orator' Hunt to speak; cavalry charges the crowd; at least 18 killed, hundreds injured — including women
Government response: Six Acts further restrict press and assembly; Cato Street Conspiracy 1820 used to justify repression
Reform pressure builds: Catholic Emancipation 1829 shows reform is possible; July Revolution in France 1830 raises fears of revolution at home
The Great Reform Act 1832: redistributes seats away from rotten boroughs, creates a £10 householder franchise — adds ~217,000 voters but excludes most working men

Working-class disappointment: Chartism, founded 1838 — the People's Charter and Six Points (universal male suffrage, secret ballot, equal constituencies, paid MPs, no property qualification, annual parliaments)
Three petitions: 1839 (1.3m signatures), 1842 (3.3m), 1848 — all rejected. Newport Rising November 1839: at least 22 Chartists killed by troops

Why Chartism 'failed' but mattered: didn't win in its own moment, but five of six points eventually became law (1858, 1867, 1872, 1884, 1911); pioneered mass organised working-class politics; provided a model for later trade unionism
lessons.exam_focus: 8-mark 'explain the significance of Chartism' — at the time vs over time.
lessons.factor_thread: Economy (post-war distress, industrialisation), ideas (franchise, democracy), communication (Northern Star newspaper, mass petitioning), government (repression and concession).

lessons.title: Anti-Slavery, Anti-Corn Law, and Reform Campaigners, c1780-1846
lessons.description: Three campaigning movements that proved Parliament could be moved by organised public pressure.
spec_bullets_covered: Protest and change: campaigning groups and their methods and impact, including the Anti-Slavery movement; the Anti-Corn Law League; factory reformers; social reformers
core_content: Anti-Slavery: Quaker networks from the 1760s; Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade founded 1787; Wilberforce introduces parliamentary bills; Olaudah Equiano's autobiography (1789) gives formerly enslaved voices to British readers; mass petitioning and the sugar boycott
Two-stage victory: Slave Trade Act 1807 (banning the trade), Slavery Abolition Act 1833 (banning the institution; £20m compensation paid to slave-owners, not the enslaved)
Anti-Corn Law League founded 1838 by Cobden and Bright: middle-class, free-trade, well-funded, used the railways and the penny post to coordinate nationally — a step change in pressure-group methods
Repeal of the Corn Laws 1846 by Sir Robert Peel: a triumph of organised non-electoral lobbying
Factory reform: Lord Shaftesbury and the Ten Hours Movement; Factory Acts 1833, 1844, 1847 — reducing children's hours, banning women and children from underground mining (1842 Mines Act)
Social reformers: Edwin Chadwick (1842 Sanitary Report) — though most public-health change comes after this period
Why these matter for the thematic story: showed that organised pressure plus moral argument plus communications technology could change law without revolution
Misconception check: Wilberforce did not 'end slavery' on his own — he was the parliamentary face of a movement built by Quakers, freed Africans, and a national petition campaign
lessons.exam_focus: 4-mark 'two ways the Anti-Slavery and Anti-Corn Law campaigns were similar' — methods or outcomes.
lessons.factor_thread: Religion (Quaker networks), ideas (rights, free trade), communication (penny post, petitioning), the role of the individual (Wilberforce, Cobden).

lessons.title: The Rise of Trade Unions: Tolpuddle to New Unionism, 1834-1889
lessons.description: From an oath under a Dorset tree to dockers shutting down London — how working people built collective power.
spec_bullets_covered: Workers movements: the development of trade unionism and its impact, including Grand National Consolidation Trades Union (GNCTU), Tolpuddle Martyrs, New Model Unions and new unionism, including the match girls' and dockers' strikes
core_content: Combination Acts 1799-1800 and their repeal 1824-25: unions are technically legal but state-suspicious
Robert Owen's Grand National Consolidated Trades Union (GNCTU), 1834: an attempt at a single national union — collapses within a year, but proves the appetite

Tolpuddle Martyrs 1834: six Dorset farm workers led by George Loveless form a friendly society and swear a secret oath; sentenced to seven years' transportation under an obscure 1797 law; mass petition of 800,000 signatures and London demonstrations force their pardon by 1836
New Model Unions 1850s-60s: skilled craft unions (engineers, carpenters) — respectable, well-funded, focused on benefits and bargaining; recognised by 1871 Trade Union Act

New Unionism late 1880s: unionising unskilled workers — match girls' strike at Bryant & May 1888 (led by Annie Besant's exposure of phossy jaw); London Dock Strike 1889 (the 'dockers' tanner', 100,000 out, victory)
Impact: TUC founded 1868; trade unions become a recognised political force; Labour Representation Committee 1900 → Labour Party 1906
Compare to Chartism: trade unions chose economic action (strikes) over constitutional petitioning — and won concrete gains
key_individuals_groups: George Loveless and the Tolpuddle Martyrs
lessons.exam_focus: 8-mark 'explain the development of trade unionism between 1834 and 1889'.
lessons.factor_thread: Economy (industrial wages), the role of the individual (Loveless, Besant), government (legal recognition then restriction), communication (mass petitioning, press campaigns).

lessons.title: Votes for Women: Suffragists, Suffragettes, and 1918
lessons.description: Two movements, two methods, one delayed victory — and a hard look at what actually changed the law.
spec_bullets_covered: Women's rights: the campaign for women's suffrage, reasons, methods and responses; role of individuals, including the Pankhursts; the reasons for the extension of the franchise and its impact; progress towards equality in the second half of the 20th century
core_content: Why women didn't have the vote: legal coverture, separate spheres ideology, fears that women voters would 'unbalance' politics
Suffragists: NUWSS founded 1897 under Millicent Fawcett — peaceful, constitutional methods, petitions, lobbying, by 1914 ~50,000 members
Suffragettes: WSPU founded 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst — 'Deeds not words'; window-smashing, arson, hunger strikes, the Cat and Mouse Act 1913, Emily Davison's death at the Derby 1913
Government response: imprisonment, force-feeding; Asquith's hostility; some movement under Lloyd George
WWI 1914-18: WSPU suspends militancy; 1.7m women in war work by 1917; suffragists keep campaigning
Representation of the People Act 1918: votes for women over 30 with property qualification (~8.4m women), and all men over 21 — the franchise quadruples
Equal Franchise Act 1928: votes for women on equal terms with men at 21
Towards equality post-1945: Equal Pay Act 1970, Sex Discrimination Act 1975, Equality Act 2010 — but the gender pay gap and political under-representation persist
Misconception check: militancy alone didn't win the vote; war service, suffragist constitutional pressure, and the political need to enfranchise returning male soldiers all mattered
lessons.exam_focus: 16-mark factors essay practice: 'Have the actions of individuals been the main factor in achieving votes for women?' — Pankhursts and Fawcett vs war, government, ideas.
lessons.factor_thread: Role of the individual (Pankhursts, Fawcett), war (1914-18), ideas (equality), government, communication (Votes for Women newspaper).

lessons.title: Workers' Rights: General Strike to Thatcher, 1926-1990
lessons.description: From nine days that nearly stopped Britain to legislation that broke union power — the long arc of organised labour.
spec_bullets_covered: Workers' rights: the General Strike (1926), actions, reactions and impact; trade union reform in the late 20th century
core_content: Background: post-WWI slump, return to gold standard 1925 over-values the pound, mine owners demand wage cuts and longer hours
The Samuel Commission 1926 rejects nationalisation, recommends wage cuts; mine owners lock workers out 1 May
General Strike 3-12 May 1926: ~1.7 million workers out across transport, print, iron and steel; TUC General Council leads it
Government response: Baldwin's emergency measures, OMS (Organisation for the Maintenance of Supplies), the BBC under government influence, troops on the streets
Collapse: TUC calls strike off unconditionally on day 9; miners stay out and are starved back by November
Impact: Trade Disputes and Trade Unions Act 1927 — sympathy strikes outlawed, civil-service unions banned from TUC; union membership drops from 8.3m (1920) to ~4.4m (1933)
Mid-century: post-war consensus, full employment, trade unions inside government from 1940s-1970s; 'In Place of Strife' 1969 fails; 1974 Industrial Relations Act repealed
Winter of Discontent 1978-79: strikes across public services contribute to Labour's defeat
Thatcher's reforms 1980, 1982, 1984: ballots before strikes, end of closed shop, no secondary picketing; Miners' Strike 1984-85 — defeat of NUM under Arthur Scargill
Long-term: union membership halves from 1979 to 2000; collective bargaining shrinks; balance of power shifts decisively to capital
lessons.exam_focus: 8-mark 'explain the significance of the 1926 General Strike' — at the time vs over time.
lessons.factor_thread: Economy (industrial decline), government (legislative response), communication (BBC, newspapers), ideas (right to strike vs public interest).

lessons.title: Minority Rights: Windrush, Brixton and Beyond, 1948-Present
lessons.description: How post-war immigration, racial discrimination, urban uprising and inquiry built modern minority-rights law.
spec_bullets_covered: Minority rights: the development of multi-racial society since the Second World War; discrimination, protest and reform; the Brixton Riots, their impact, including the Scarman Report
core_content: 1948 British Nationality Act and the Empire Windrush: Caribbean migration to fill labour shortages; subsequent migration from South Asia and East Africa
Discrimination in housing, employment and policing: 'No Blacks, No Irish, No Dogs'; 1958 Notting Hill riots show white-on-Black violence
Legislative response: Race Relations Acts 1965, 1968, 1976 — outlawing direct discrimination and creating the Commission for Racial Equality; Bristol Bus Boycott 1963 forces local change
1970s-80s tensions: Stop and Search ('sus laws'), economic recession, far-right activity, deteriorating police-community relations in inner cities
Brixton Riots April 1981: triggered by Operation Swamp 81 (1,000+ stops in 5 days under sus laws); 3 days of unrest, 300 police and 65 civilians injured, 28 buildings burned, no fatalities
Toxteth, Moss Side, Handsworth riots through summer 1981

The Scarman Report (Nov 1981): identified 'racial disadvantage' but rejected institutional racism; urged community policing, recruitment of Black officers, scrapping of sus laws — Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984
Stephen Lawrence murder 1993 and Macpherson Report 1999: introduces the term 'institutional racism' into UK policy
21st century: Equality Act 2010; Black Lives Matter UK 2020 (Colston statue, Bristol); ongoing debates over Windrush scandal and policing
Misconception check: the Scarman Report stopped short of calling the Met institutionally racist — it took Macpherson 18 years later to do that
lessons.exam_focus: 8-mark 'explain the significance of the Brixton Riots' — at the time vs over time.
lessons.factor_thread: Government (Race Relations Acts, Scarman, Macpherson), economy (1981 unemployment), ideas (equality, anti-racism), communication (broadcast media, social media for BLM).

lessons.title: Synthesis: Factors Across 850 Years — Cracking the 16-Mark Essay
lessons.description: Threading the seven factors and the role of individuals from 1170 to today, and rehearsing the highest-stakes question type.
spec_bullets_covered: synthesis across all four parts; thematic factor essay technique
core_content: Tracking each factor across all four parts: a worked grid showing where war, religion, chance, government, communication, the economy, ideas, and the role of the individual matter most
Why some factors dominate certain eras (religion 1381-1689; ideas of representation 1640-1832; the economy and communication 1832-present) and why this pattern matters
The 16-mark essay rubric in detail: AO1 knowledge, AO2 explanation, AO2 analysis and judgement
How to plan in 5 minutes: name the factor, list two examples for it, list two examples against it, choose a defensible judgement
Worked example essay on a Pankhurst-style factor question (the role of individuals): top-band paragraph structure
Worked example essay on a religion-style factor question: showing range across at least two of the four parts
Common pitfalls in real exam scripts: single-period coverage, list-not-judgement, ignoring the named factor, treating individuals as causes in isolation
Specialist vocabulary checklist for SPaG: feudalism, franchise, enfranchisement, parliamentary supremacy, mass movement, direct action, institutional racism
Final factor judgement framework: 'Factor X mattered most when [conditions], but factor Y was more important when [other conditions], because [evidence] — overall, [reasoned conclusion]'
lessons.exam_focus: 16-mark factors essay full walkthrough with two contrasting prompts; band-by-band paragraph rewriting.
lessons.factor_thread: All seven factors revisited; this lesson is the closing index.

teaching_brief.thematic_framing: This is a ~850-year thematic study of the changing relationship between citizen and state in Britain, from feudal kingship under Henry II to twenty-first-century minority rights movements. The seven AQA factors — war, religion, chance, government, communication, the economy, ideas (equality, democracy, representation), and the role of the individual — are the spine of the unit. Every lesson should foreground how one or more of these factors drove a moment of challenge to authority, and how authority responded. Students need to be able to step back and trace a factor (e.g. ideas, or the role of the individual) across all four parts of the course; lessons therefore close with a 'thread' callback that names the factor in play and previews where it will reappear later. The thematic study is assessed on Paper 2 Section A through four question types — the 4-mark 'two ways similar or different', the 8-mark 'explain the significance', the 8-mark 'explain a development', and the 16-mark factors essay. The factors essay is the highest-stakes question on the unit and the one most students lose marks on, so judgement against the named factor is rehearsed from lesson 1, not just at the end.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Magna Carta 'gave rights to the British people' or 'started democracy'.
common_misconceptions.correction: Magna Carta was a peace treaty between King John and a small group of rebel barons. Its terms protected the elite — the nobles, the Church and the City of London — not ordinary subjects. The famous 'free man' clauses applied to free men only, who were a minority of the population. The long-term democratic legacy (rule of law, limits on executive power) was constructed by later generations, particularly in the seventeenth century — it was not the document's intent in 1215.
common_misconceptions.source: UK Parliament 'Magna Carta legacy' pages; British Library Magna Carta blog (parliament.uk and bl.uk)

common_misconceptions.misconception: The Chartists 'won' because they got their demands.
common_misconceptions.correction: All six points except annual parliaments were eventually conceded — but over the following 80 years, by parliaments responding to entirely new pressures (1867, 1872, 1884, 1911, 1918). At the time, Chartism was rejected three times by Parliament, the 1839 Newport Rising was crushed with at least 22 dead, leaders were transported, and the movement collapsed by 1848. Chartism's significance lies in pioneering mass organised working-class politics, not in winning concessions in its own moment.
common_misconceptions.source: UK Parliament 'Chartist movement' overview; The National Archives 'What was Chartism?' (parliament.uk and nationalarchives.gov.uk)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Suffragettes and suffragists were the same movement, or the suffragettes won the vote single-handed.
common_misconceptions.correction: Suffragists (NUWSS, Millicent Fawcett, founded 1897) used peaceful, constitutional methods — petitions, lobbying, public meetings — and were the larger movement. Suffragettes (WSPU, the Pankhursts, founded 1903) used militant direct action — window-smashing, arson, hunger strikes. The two groups overlapped early on but split after 1912. Most historians now argue women's war work, the 1918 redrawing of the franchise to enfranchise male soldiers, and decades of suffragist constitutional pressure mattered as much as militancy in delivering the 1918 Representation of the People Act.
common_misconceptions.source: UK Parliament 'Women and the vote' pages; The National Archives 'What methods did the Suffragettes use to gain the vote?' (parliament.uk and nationalarchives.gov.uk)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Modern protest is more violent than protest in the past.
common_misconceptions.correction: By any measure of state violence and casualties, earlier protests were far more dangerous: Peterloo (1819) killed at least 18 protesters, the Newport Rising (1839) killed 22 Chartists, troops fired on rioters during the 1831 Reform Act crisis, and the Tolpuddle leaders were transported to Australia for taking an oath. Twentieth-century protest is by comparison more organised and less lethally policed. Brixton 1981 was a flashpoint of state-community breakdown, but resulted in 0 fatalities; Black Lives Matter UK protests in 2020 were overwhelmingly peaceful.
common_misconceptions.source: The National Archives 'Protest in the 20th century'; The National Archives 'Peterloo Massacre' resources (nationalarchives.gov.uk)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Individuals like Wilberforce, Pankhurst or Cromwell 'caused' major change on their own.
common_misconceptions.correction: AQA explicitly tests the role of the individual as one factor among many, and examiner reports flag that students who isolate individuals as sole causes lose AO2 analytical marks. Wilberforce was the parliamentary face of an abolition movement built by Quakers, freed slaves like Olaudah Equiano, and a national petition campaign. The Pankhursts were one strand of a multi-decade campaign. Cromwell rose because the New Model Army and the Levellers existed, not because of personal genius alone. Always frame individuals within the wider conditions that made them effective.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA principal examiner reports for GCSE History 8145 Paper 2 Section A factor essays (aqa.org.uk)

common_misconceptions.misconception: The English Civil War was a fight for democracy.
common_misconceptions.correction: The Civil War (1642-1651) was fought between Parliament and Charles I over royal authority, religion and finance — most parliamentarians wanted a constitutional monarchy, not a republic. Radical democratic ideas emerged inside it, particularly through the New Model Army and the Leveller pamphlets (1647 'Agreement of the People'), but the Levellers were suppressed by Cromwell, and the Restoration in 1660 reinstated the monarchy. The democratic legacy is real but indirect: the war established that a king who breaks the law can be removed, and seeded ideas later generations would draw on.
common_misconceptions.source: UK Parliament 'Civil War' pages; English Heritage 'The English Civil Wars' (parliament.uk and english-heritage.org.uk)

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: 16-mark factors essay: the named factor (e.g. religion, ideas, the role of individuals) must be addressed first, weighed against at least two other factors, with examples drawn from at least two of the four parts of the course. teaching_brief.unit_overview: A thematic study covering c790 to the present — the longest sweep on the spec, around 1,200 years. Students trace how invasion, settlement, migration and empire have shaped Britain's people and identity. The four AQA-named parts run chronologically: Conquered and Conquerors (Vikings to the Hundred Years' War), Looking West (sugar, slavery, North America, Huguenots, Highland clearances, Ulster), Expansion and Empire (India, Africa, Irish/Jewish migration, internal migration), and Britain in the 20th Century (end of empire, Windrush, Commonwealth migration, Europe). Throughout, students weigh seven named factors: war, religion, government, economic resources, science and technology, ideas (imperialism, social Darwinism, civilisation), and the role of individuals. The unit assesses second-order concepts of significance, similarity and difference, change over time, and the interplay of factors.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students believe migration to Britain is essentially a post-1948 (Windrush) phenomenon — the longest unit on the spec is precisely a corrective to this. Black presence in Britain pre-dates Windrush by centuries; the unit begins in c790 with Viking arrivals.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: David Olusoga, Black and British: A Forgotten History (Pan Macmillan, 2016/2021); BBC documentary series of the same name; AQA spec rationale 3.3.2 AC

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students conflate the three terms and use them interchangeably. The spec demands precision: empire (the political system of rule), colonialism (the practice of settling and exploiting territory), imperialism (the ideology justifying expansion, including social Darwinism and 'civilising mission').
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA spec line 1333 explicitly names imperialism and social Darwinism as factors students must distinguish; AQA principal examiner reports flag this on 16-mark factor essays

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students treat 'British' as a fixed identity that migrants joined or threatened. The spec's framing — 'how the identity of the people of Britain has been shaped by their interaction with the wider world' — is that British identity is itself the product of repeated migration (Anglo-Saxons, Vikings, Normans, Huguenots, Irish, Jews, Caribbean, South Asian).
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA spec lines 1312-1317; David Olusoga's argument in Black and British (2016) that British history has always been multicultural

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.topic: Windrush as the 'start' of Black British history
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students treat 22 June 1948 as Year Zero for Black Britain. In fact people of African descent have been documented in Britain since the Roman period, with established communities from the 1500s. Olusoga: post-war migration was unprecedented in scale but did not mark the beginnings of Black British history.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: David Olusoga, Black and British (2016/2021 edition with new chapter on Windrush scandal); Royal Museums Greenwich and BBC documentary commentary

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students present the Atlantic slave trade as a natural extension of European exploration rather than a deliberate, contested, profit-driven system that abolitionists campaigned against for decades before the 1807 Slave Trade Act and 1833 Slavery Abolition Act.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Historic England Timeline of the Transatlantic Slave Trade and Abolition; UK Parliament Heritage Collections on the Transatlantic Slave Trade

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.topic: Empire as economically beneficial to all
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students assume empire enriched Britain straightforwardly and improved colonised societies. The historiography is contested: Niall Ferguson's case for empire's modernising effects sits against Caroline Elkins, Shashi Tharoor and others on famine, dispossession, the Bengal famine, the Mau Mau detentions and the long economic drain on India.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Niall Ferguson, Empire: How Britain Made the Modern World (2003); Caroline Elkins, Britain's Gulag (2005) and Legacy of Violence (2022); AQA examiner reports flag students writing one-sided defences or condemnations

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Essays often Anglocentrically describe what was 'done to' migrants without showing migrants' own agency — Claudia Jones founding the West Indian Gazette and the indoor Caribbean Carnival in 1959 (response to the 1958 Notting Hill attacks), Gandhi's Indian National Congress strategy, Nkrumah's Convention People's Party, Kenyatta's KANU.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA examiner reports on 16-mark factor essays; The National Archives 'Empire Windrush: The Notting Hill Carnival' resource on Claudia Jones

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 8-mark significance question rewards both significance at the time and significance over time. Students who only address the immediate impact of an event (e.g. Windrush 1948 docking at Tilbury) cap themselves; top-band answers also explain its long-term legacy (1981 Nationality Act, 2018 Windrush scandal, Notting Hill Carnival, multicultural Britain).
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section A 8-mark significance questions (8145/2A/C series)

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 16-mark factor essay names ONE factor (e.g. 'war', 'government', 'role of individuals') and asks students to weigh it against others. Top-band answers explicitly address the named factor across at least two of the four AQA parts and reach a substantiated overall judgement — not a list of factors with no comparison.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 Paper 2 Section A; AQA examiner reports flagging factor-list responses as a recurring issue

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 4-mark 'similar or different' question requires TWO ways and concrete supporting detail from across the period, not generic claims. Comparing across vastly different periods (Vikings vs Windrush, Huguenots vs Ugandan Asians) is consistently the hardest comparison skill at GCSE.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA spec section 4.4.2; Cambridge Assessment Network research on history examinations highlighting comparative judgement as the hardest GCSE skill

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 8-mark 'explain a development' question rewards causal narrative with consequences, not pure description. A development is a process across time (e.g. how the East India Company's role developed from trading post to political ruler) — students who narrate without explaining the consequences of each stage cap below the top band.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section A 8-mark explain-a-development questions

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Students must use specialist historical vocabulary (Danelaw, sepoy, abolitionist, dominion, Commonwealth, imperialism) accurately to access SPaG marks and the top mark band on extended responses.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA spec section 4.4.3 SPaG performance descriptors

teaching_brief.exam_paper_context: This is a Paper 2 Section A thematic study, examined alongside the British depth study (Section B) in a 2-hour Paper 2 worth 84 marks total. The thematic component is worth 40 marks (plus 3 SPaG), assessed through four question types: 4-mark Two Ways Similar or Different, 8-mark Explain Significance, 8-mark Explain a Development, and 16-mark Factors Essay (the named-factor judgement). All four questions span the full c790-present period, so students cannot get away with revising only one part of the unit.
