thematic_threads: Was this really a 'Golden Age'? Test the label against poverty, religious persecution, the slave-trading voyages of Hawkins, and the failure at Roanoke — not just against theatre, fashion and Drake's gold.
How did Elizabeth survive without an army or a husband? Track court patronage, ministerial talent (Cecil, Walsingham), Parliament management, and image-making (Gloriana, the Armada portrait).

How did religious threat reshape the regime over 35 years? From cautious 1568 settlement, through 1569 Northern Rebellion and 1570 excommunication, to harsh recusancy laws, the execution of Mary in 1587 and war with Spain in 1588.

How does The Globe (the 2026 historic environment site) sit inside all of this? It is the visible artefact of patronage (Lord Chamberlain's Men), of the gentry/middling sort with money to spend, and of the cultural confidence — and the Puritan/civic backlash — that the period produced.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students treat 'Golden Age' as a finding rather than a label invented later. They miss that the same decade gave us Drake's voyages and a sharp rise in vagrancy, harsher recusancy laws and English involvement in the slave trade.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 Paper 2 Section B noting weaker responses to Golden Age questions; History Today, 'Poverty in Elizabethan England'.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.topic: Mary Queen of Scots vs Mary I
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students confuse Mary Queen of Scots (Elizabeth's Catholic Stuart cousin, executed 1587) with Mary I (Elizabeth's Tudor half-sister, who died in 1558 before this depth study even begins).
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 Paper 2 Section B Elizabethan questions.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students say the Armada 'was beaten by the weather' and stop there. They miss the role of English fireships at Calais, the lighter and faster English ship design, the breakdown of Spanish supply, and Spanish strategic overreach.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 Paper 2 Section B; Royal Museums Greenwich teaching resources on the Armada.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students assume everyone loved Elizabethan theatre. In fact Puritans, the City of London authorities and many town councils saw playhouses as sites of plague spread, vagrancy, prostitution and disorder, which is why The Globe was built outside the City walls in Southwark.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Shakespeare's Globe — 'Playhouses' and 'The Globe'; History Today archive on Puritanism and theatre closures.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students describe the site (here The Globe) without ever linking back to the wider events and developments of the period — which is the second-order question prompt the marker is looking for.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 for Paper 2 Section B; AQA published answers and commentaries for 8145/2BC.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students treat 'patronage' as bribery rather than the routine system through which Elizabeth bound nobles, soldiers and even sailors (Drake, Raleigh) to the Crown. Without that, Essex's rebellion in 1601 doesn't make sense — he had just lost his sweet wine monopoly.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: History Today, 'The Fall of Essex' and 'The Execution of the Earl of Essex'.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 16-mark historic environment essay must explicitly link the specified site (The Globe in 2026) to wider events and developments of the period — describing the playhouse alone, however accurately, caps the response below the top band.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 for Paper 2 Section B; AQA answers and commentaries for 8145/2BC.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Top-band responses on Mary Queen of Scots, the Northern Rebellion and the Armada bring in interaction: Mary's existence drove the plots, the plots drove the harsher recusancy laws, the laws drove some Catholics to Spain — leading to the Armada. Lower-band answers treat each event as standalone.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 Paper 2 Section B Elizabethan questions; AQA published commentary.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On the 8-mark significance question, the strongest answers explain significance both at the time and over time — for example, Drake's circumnavigation mattered in 1580 (knighthood, gold, blow to Spain) and afterwards (English claim to global trade, model for later voyages, Roanoke).
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 significance question across Paper 2 papers.

pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.note: Sequence the religious thread chronologically across Lessons 5-8 so that students see causation: 1568 settlement → 1569 Northern Rebellion → 1570 excommunication → 1580s plots → 1587 Mary executed → 1588 Armada. Examiner reports show students who learn these as separate topics struggle to write the 8-mark explain question.
pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B Elizabethan; EEF metacognition guidance on modelling causal chains.

pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.note: Front-load the 'Golden Age' question rather than leaving it to revision. Lesson 9 (rise of gentry/fashion) and Lesson 10 (poverty/Poor Laws) sit deliberately next to each other so students can already weigh evidence on both sides before they see an exam question that asks 'how far'.
pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — explicit teaching of disciplinary judgement vocabulary; History Today, 'Poverty in Elizabethan England'.

pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.note: Lesson 12 (theatre and attitudes) is engineered as the bridge into Lesson 13 (The Globe historic environment). Teaching attitudes to the theatre — Puritan opposition, City of London bans, why Bankside was outside city jurisdiction — gives students the wider-period material the 16-marker rewards.
pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 — historic environment connects site to period; Shakespeare's Globe teaching resources on Bankside playhouses.

pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.note: Cambridge Assessment notes that comparative judgement is the hardest skill at GCSE — schedule retrieval and worked examples on the 16-mark historic environment essay specifically, not just on the 8-mark questions, because students rarely meet that essay format anywhere else in the course.
pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.source: Cambridge Assessment Network and Research, history specifications and reports archive.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Elizabeth I
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Queen of England 1558-1603, central figure of the entire depth study.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William Cecil (Lord Burghley)
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Elizabeth's principal minister and Lord Treasurer; ran government for almost the whole reign.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert Cecil
key_individuals_and_groups.role: William Cecil's son; succeeded him as principal minister; opposed Essex in 1601.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sir Francis Walsingham
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Principal Secretary and spymaster; uncovered the Babington Plot.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Court favourite turned rebel; led the failed 1601 rebellion; executed for treason.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Mary, Queen of Scots
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Catholic Stuart claimant to the English throne; held in England 1568-1587; executed at Fotheringhay.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sir Francis Drake
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Sea Dog, circumnavigator (1577-1580), vice-admiral against the Armada.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sir John Hawkins
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Naval commander, slave trader, redesigner of the English fleet that beat the Armada.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sir Walter Raleigh
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Court favourite and patron of the failed Roanoke colony in North America.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: King Philip II of Spain
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Catholic king who launched the 1588 Armada against England.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Pope Pius V
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Issued the 1570 papal bull 'Regnans in Excelsis' excommunicating Elizabeth.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Anthony Babington
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Catholic gentleman whose 1586 plot to free Mary and assassinate Elizabeth led to Mary's execution.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: James Burbage and Richard Burbage
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Father-and-son theatre family; built The Theatre in Shoreditch and then The Globe in Southwark.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William Shakespeare
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Playwright and part-owner (sharer) in the Lord Chamberlain's Men at The Globe.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Lord Chamberlain's Men
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Acting company that built and performed at The Globe; patronised by the Lord Chamberlain at court.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Catholic recusants
key_individuals_and_groups.role: English Catholics who refused to attend Anglican services after the 1559 settlement; faced rising fines and persecution from the 1570s.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Puritans
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Hardline Protestants who wanted further reform and were the loudest critics of theatre, fashion and court ritual.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The gentry
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Landowning class below the nobility whose rise reshaped Parliament, county government and fashion.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The vagrant poor
key_individuals_and_groups.role: The 'sturdy beggars' and 'impotent poor' whose growing numbers drove the 1572, 1576 and 1598 Poor Laws.

article_units.name: Norman England, c1066-c1100
article_units.subtitle: Conquest, control, the Domesday Book, the feudal system and the reform of the Church.
article_units.spec_section_focus: British depth study with historic environment, the Norman Conquest and its aftermath

site_2026.location: East Sussex, on the south coast of England
site_2026.source: aqa.org.uk/news/gcse-history-historic-environment-sites-2026-2028 (sites announced for 2026-2028 cycle: 2026 Pevensey Castle, 2027 The Battle of Hastings, 2028 The White Tower)
site_2026.why_relevant: Pevensey was William's landing site on 28 September 1066, where he sheltered his fleet of c.700 ships inside a Roman fort and built his first English fortification — directly anchoring the conquest narrative to a specific physical place. The castle was then granted to Robert of Mortain (William's half-brother), who turned it into a permanent stone castle and used the Roman walls as his outer bailey. In 1088 it was the focus of a six-week siege by William II (Rufus) when Robert backed Robert Curthose's rebellion — making the site relevant across all three reigns of the spec (William I, William II) and across all four parts of the depth study: conquest (Part 1), castles and feudal landholding (Parts 1 & 2), Church links via St Nicolas's Church inside the bailey (Part 3), and the historic environment essay itself (Part 4).
key_features_for_essays: Roman fort (Anderida, c.AD 290) reused as the outer wall — illustrates Norman opportunism in repurposing existing fortifications
Coastal peninsula location controlling Channel crossing — strategic for communication with Normandy
Inner bailey ditch and stone keep added under Robert of Mortain — shows transition from temporary timber fortification to permanent Norman stronghold
1088 siege by William Rufus — links the site to William II's struggle to secure his inheritance against his brother Robert Curthose
Connections to the wider conquest: William's first foothold, granted as patronage to a tenant-in-chief, garrisoned during revolts

historic_environment_dropped_for_v1.reason: L13 anchored on Pevensey Castle (rotating 2026 site)

article_units.content_agent_guardrails_for_he: Do NOT reference the AQA-specified 2026 historic environment site for this option (e.g. Globe, Pevensey, Caernarfon, Ham House). The site rotates yearly and we are deferring that content. Period-general castle/theatre/site content is fine where naturally part of the topic.

lessons.title: Edward's Death and the Succession Crisis of 1066
lessons.description: Childless king, four claimants, and a kingdom on the edge — why January 1066 set everything in motion.
lessons.teaching_focus: Trace Edward the Confessor's reign and his ambiguous succession promises (William 1051, Harold's deathbed gesture, Hardrada's claim via Cnut). Explain why each of the four claimants — Harold, William, Hardrada, Edgar Atheling — believed they had the better case, and why the Witan went for Harold.
key_content: Edward the Confessor's reign and childlessness
1051 promise to William
Harold Godwinson's coronation 6 January 1066
Harald Hardrada and Tostig Godwinson
Edgar Atheling and the Witan's choice
Why the throne mattered: wealth and prestige of England in 1066
lessons.misconception_to_target: That Harold was a usurper. From the Anglo-Saxon perspective the Witan's choice was legitimate; the Norman framing of Harold-as-oathbreaker is post-1066 propaganda.

lessons.title: Stamford Bridge and Hastings: the Battles of 1066
lessons.description: Two battles in three weeks: how the Vikings, the English and the Normans collided in autumn 1066.
lessons.teaching_focus: Run through Hardrada's invasion at Fulford and the English victory at Stamford Bridge (25 Sep), then the rapid march south, William's landing at Pevensey (28 Sep), and the Battle of Hastings (14 Oct). Stress Anglo-Saxon and Norman tactics — shield wall vs cavalry/archers — and the close-run nature of Hastings.
key_content: Battle of Fulford and Stamford Bridge
Anglo-Saxon shield wall and housecarls
William's landing at Pevensey
Hastings: terrain, feigned retreats, Harold's death
Why the battle was close-run, not inevitable
Tactics and military innovations: cavalry, archers, castles
lessons.misconception_to_target: That Norman cavalry made victory inevitable. The shield wall held until late afternoon; Harold's death (probably an arrow + a knight, not an arrow alone) and the resulting collapse decided it.

lessons.title: From Hastings to Coronation: William Takes the Throne
lessons.description: How William turned a battlefield win into a crown — and what Christmas Day 1066 actually looked like.
lessons.teaching_focus: Cover the post-Hastings march via Dover, Canterbury, Wallingford and Berkhamsted; the submission of Edgar Atheling and the Witan; the coronation at Westminster Abbey on 25 December 1066 and the riot outside; William's early conciliation policies (confirming Anglo-Saxon law, keeping some English officials).
key_content: Post-Hastings march and submissions
Berkhamsted: surrender of Edgar Atheling
Coronation at Westminster Abbey, 25 Dec 1066
Crowd panic and houses burned outside the abbey
Early conciliation of English nobility
William's first castles in London (the Tower) and elsewhere
lessons.misconception_to_target: That coronation = total control. William ruled only the south-east in early 1067; the Midlands, North and Welsh borderlands were still effectively independent.

lessons.title: Resistance and Revolt, 1067-1071
lessons.description: Kent, the South-West, the North, the Fens — five years of revolts that nearly unmade the conquest.
lessons.teaching_focus: Walk through the revolts: Kent and Eustace of Boulogne (1067), Exeter (1068), Edwin and Morcar in the North (1068), the Danish-backed northern revolt and the harrying of York (1069), Hereward at Ely (1070-71). Show how each revolt prompted more castles and harsher reprisals.
key_content: Eustace of Boulogne and Kent, 1067
Exeter siege, 1068
Earls Edwin and Morcar in the North
Danish fleet and the sack of York 1069
Hereward the Wake at Ely 1070-71
Castle-building as a response to revolt
lessons.misconception_to_target: That resistance was uncoordinated and doomed. Several revolts came close to forcing William out — the 1069 northern revolt with Danish fleet support was the most dangerous moment of his reign.

lessons.title: The Harrying of the North, 1069-1070
lessons.description: William's scorched-earth answer to rebellion — and a debate historians still cannot settle.
lessons.teaching_focus: Detail the winter campaign of 1069-70: villages razed, livestock killed, food stores destroyed across Yorkshire and beyond. Use Orderic Vitalis's '100,000 dead' alongside Domesday's 'waste' entries to teach historiographical caution. Stress the political effect: the North was not seriously rebellious again under William I.
key_content: The 1069 northern revolt and Danish fleet
William's winter campaign
Scale and methods of destruction
Orderic Vitalis and John of Worcester accounts
Domesday 'waste' entries
Modern historiographical debate (Hugh Thomas vs older readings)
Long-term effect on northern landholding
lessons.misconception_to_target: That '100,000 dead' is a fact. It is a chronicle figure written decades later by a writer who hated cruelty. Modern historians treat it as evidence of perceived horror, not a head-count.

lessons.title: Feudalism and the Norman Land Settlement
lessons.description: Land for service, lord and vassal, knights' fees: how William rebuilt English society as a pyramid.
lessons.teaching_focus: Explain the feudal pyramid (king > tenants-in-chief > sub-tenants > peasants) using concrete cases: Robert of Mortain holding Pevensey of the king, sub-infeudating manors to his own knights. Cover military service obligations, knights' fees, patronage, and the dispossession of the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy. Flag the historiographical debate (Reynolds) — students learn the working model, but understand it's a model.
key_content: The feudal pyramid: king, tenants-in-chief, sub-tenants, peasants
Knights' fees and military service obligation
Sub-infeudation and patronage
Dispossession of Anglo-Saxon thegns by 1086
Robert of Mortain as a case study
Reynolds critique: 'feudalism' as a model not a system
lessons.misconception_to_target: That William invented feudalism. Norman France already had this pattern; William transplanted and intensified it. And — per Reynolds — calling it 'a system' overstates its tidiness.

lessons.title: Castles: Instruments of Conquest and Control
lessons.description: How c.500 motte-and-bailey castles and a few stone keeps held down a kingdom of two million.
lessons.teaching_focus: Cover the spread of castles from c.50 in 1066 to c.500 by 1100. Distinguish motte-and-bailey (timber, fast to build) from stone keeps (Tower of London's White Tower, Colchester). Stress castles as instruments of conquest first — projection of lordly power, garrisoning towns, controlling river crossings — and only secondarily defensive. Foreshadow Pevensey as the unit's specified site.
key_content: Castles before 1066 (rare in Anglo-Saxon England)
Motte-and-bailey design and rapid construction
Tower of London and the White Tower
Castle siting: river crossings, town centres, road junctions
Castles as projection of power, not just defence
Sample sites: Berkhamsted, York, Lincoln, Pevensey
lessons.misconception_to_target: That castles were only defensive. They were political tools — visible threats to local populations and bases for armed retinues to project power outward.

lessons.title: Norman Government, Justice and the Anglo-Saxon Inheritance
lessons.description: Sheriffs, hundred courts, ordeals and 'murdrum': what the Normans kept and what they bolted on.
lessons.teaching_focus: Show what the Normans inherited (shires, hundreds, sheriffs, the writ, Anglo-Saxon law codes) and what they added (forest law, the murdrum fine, French as the language of the elite courts, expanded royal justice via itinerant officials). Compare Anglo-Saxon and Norman aristocracies and their different cultures of authority.
key_content: Inherited Anglo-Saxon government: shires, hundreds, sheriffs, writs
Anglo-Saxon and Norman aristocracies compared
Norman additions: forest law, murdrum fine
Justice and the legal system: ordeals, trial by combat
Inheritance law (primogeniture vs partible)
Continuity beneath rupture (Hugh Thomas thesis)
lessons.question_type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
lessons.misconception_to_target: That Norman government was a clean break. The framework — shires, sheriffs, hundred courts — was inherited largely intact; the personnel changed.

lessons.title: The Domesday Book, 1086
lessons.description: A whole kingdom audited in two years: what William really wanted to know — and what we get to read 940 years later.
lessons.teaching_focus: Cover the 1085 Christmas council at Gloucester, the survey commissioners and procedures, the Great Domesday and Little Domesday volumes, and the speed of the operation. Dig into purposes: tax assessment (geld capacity), recording the new tenurial structure post-conquest, settling disputes between tenants-in-chief. Use real entries to model 'describe two features' practice.
key_content: 1085 Christmas council and the decision to survey
Commissioners, juries and procedure
Great and Little Domesday
Purpose: tax, tenurial record, dispute settlement
What Domesday reveals about post-conquest landholding (c.180 tenants-in-chief; <10% Anglo-Saxon survival)
Why historians treat 'waste' entries cautiously
lessons.misconception_to_target: That Domesday was a legal land registry. It was primarily fiscal and political — an audit of who held what and how much it could be taxed.

lessons.title: Daily Life: Towns, Villages and Economic Change
lessons.description: For most people the king never visited — but the new lord did. Life on the manor under Norman rule.
lessons.teaching_focus: Compare Anglo-Saxon and Norman rural and urban life: villages, manorial farming, seasonal labour, markets, towns. Cover the impact of forest law (royal hunting reserves, savage penalties), urban changes (French quarters in major towns, new market grants), economic continuity for most peasants, and the way Norman lords reshaped landscapes (parks, castles, burhs).
key_content: Anglo-Saxon village and manorial life
Towns and markets before and after 1066
French quarters in conquered towns (e.g. Norwich, Nottingham)
Forest law and royal hunting reserves
Seasonal labour and food
Continuity for most peasants beneath the Norman elite
lessons.question_type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
lessons.misconception_to_target: That Norman conquest revolutionised peasant life immediately. For most ordinary people, daily life and labour patterns continued; the lord's name and language changed at the top.

lessons.title: Lanfranc and the Reform of the English Church
lessons.description: An Italian monk, an English Church and a programme of cathedrals, councils and Norman bishops.
lessons.teaching_focus: Cover the Anglo-Saxon Church before 1066 (Stigand's pluralism, monastic centres at Worcester and Canterbury). Trace Lanfranc's appointment in 1070, his replacement of Anglo-Saxon bishops with Normans, the 1075 Council of London reorganising dioceses, the great cathedral building programme (Canterbury, Durham, St Albans, Old Sarum), and the Canterbury-vs-York primacy dispute.
key_content: Anglo-Saxon Church before 1066: structure, learning, criticisms
Stigand and his deposition 1070
Lanfranc's appointment and reform programme
Replacement of Anglo-Saxon bishops with Normans
1075 Council of London: dioceses moved to towns
Cathedral building: Canterbury, Durham, St Albans
Canterbury-York primacy dispute
lessons.misconception_to_target: That the Anglo-Saxon Church was decadent and Lanfranc cleaned it up. The pre-conquest Church had reform impulses; Lanfranc's main effect was Norman political control of personnel and a building programme that visibly stamped Norman authority.

lessons.title: Monasticism, Learning and the Investiture Controversy
lessons.description: New abbeys, new schools, Latin and the vernacular — and the row over who owns the bishops.
lessons.teaching_focus: Cover Norman monasticism: new abbeys (Battle Abbey on the Hastings field, Selby, Tewkesbury), Cluniac and Benedictine reform, monastic schools, Latin learning. Then turn to Church-state tensions: William I's relationship with the papacy (refused homage to Gregory VII), William II's exploitation of vacant Church lands, Anselm's clash with Rufus from 1093 — the English phase of the Investiture Controversy.
key_content: Norman abbey-building: Battle, Selby, Tewkesbury
Monastic life and reform
Schools, Latin and the vernacular
William I and Pope Gregory VII
Church wealth and royal exploitation under William II
Anselm's clash with William Rufus
Beginnings of the Investiture Controversy in England
lessons.misconception_to_target: That the Investiture Controversy was a continental problem only. England was drawn in from the 1090s through Anselm's struggle with Rufus over Church appointments and obedience to Rome.

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume Hastings was inevitable — that Norman cavalry and archers were always going to overwhelm a 'primitive' Anglo-Saxon shield wall. In reality the housecarls were elite, the shield wall held until late afternoon, and historians stress how close-run the battle was; Harold's death (whatever the cause) was the decisive accident.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE History 8145 examiner reports flag thin causation on Hastings; Marc Morris, The Norman Conquest (2012); English Heritage 'What Happened at the Battle of Hastings'

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat castles as purely defensive. They were instruments of conquest first — projection of lordly power, control of road junctions and river crossings, intimidation of nearby populations — and only secondarily defensive structures.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: English Heritage 'Norman Castles' overview; History Today articles on motte-and-bailey colonisation

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students think Domesday was a legal land registry to settle property disputes. Its primary purposes were fiscal (raising geld and assessing tax capacity) and political (recording the new Norman tenurial structure and tenants-in-chief), not adjudicative.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: The National Archives 'Spotlight On: Domesday Book'; History Today 'Domesday in the Middle Ages: Usage and Abusage'

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'the Normans' as one homogeneous group. William's invasion army was a coalition — Normans, Bretons, Flemings, French — and his post-conquest aristocracy reflected that mix; calling everyone 'Norman' obscures the patronage politics.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: Marc Morris, The Norman Conquest; Hugh Thomas, The English and the Normans (2003)

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students either downplay it ('just a punitive raid') or treat Orderic Vitalis's claim of 100,000 dead as straight fact. Modern historians sit between: scale of destruction was real and unprecedented, but contemporary chroniclers writing decades later inflated numbers, and Domesday's 'waste' entries are now read with caution.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: History Today 'The Harrying of the North'; Hugh Thomas's The English and the Normans

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students think 'feudalism' was a system William sat down and designed. It was a working pattern of landholding-for-service that evolved, with the king at the top, tenants-in-chief, sub-tenants and peasants — and historians now debate whether 'feudalism' as a single system even existed.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: AQA examiner commentary on weak feudal-system answers; Susan Reynolds, Fiefs and Vassals (1994)

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume the Anglo-Saxon Church was 'corrupt' and Lanfranc 'cleaned it up'. The pre-1066 Church had its own learning and reform impulses; Lanfranc's changes were as much about Norman political control (replacing bishops, building cathedrals, reorienting monasticism) as about doctrinal cleanup.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: English Heritage 'Beyond 1066: the real story of the Norman Conquest'; History Today on Lanfranc and Anselm

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On the 16-mark historic environment essay, top-band answers explicitly tie features of Pevensey Castle (Roman walls, peninsula site, inner bailey, the 1088 siege) to wider depth-study themes — conquest, control, William II's reign — rather than describing the site in isolation.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 for Paper 2 Section B; Oxford University Press blog 'How to tackle the Historic Environment question in AQA GCSE History'

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On the 8-mark 'Explain the Importance' question, students must choose two factors and weigh them — not just describe two things. Importance means consequences for the period, not just 'it happened'.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: Save My Exams summary of AQA GCSE History 8145 Q2 marking guidance (signposting only — drawn from publicly released mark schemes)

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On 4-mark 'Describe Two Features' questions, examiners reward a precise feature plus a developed sentence of detail per feature — no need for analysis, but vague labels ('the feudal system was important') score nothing.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA GCSE History 8145 Paper 2B/A mark schemes (June 2018 onwards)

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Historic environment essays consistently reward use of named features of the specific site. For Pevensey 2026, examiners will expect candidates to deploy 'Roman walls', 'inner bailey', 'Robert of Mortain', '1088 siege' as concrete anchors, not generic 'castle' language.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA released 2019 mark scheme for Pevensey Castle paper (the previous time Pevensey was the specified site)

historiography.summary: Hugh Thomas (The English and the Normans, 2003) argues for substantial Anglo-Saxon continuity — language, law, local administration, peasant life — beneath a thin Norman ruling crust. Marc Morris (The Norman Conquest, 2012) emphasises rupture — wholesale dispossession of the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy, transformation of Church personnel, the violence of the Harrying.
historiography.source: Public-facing summaries on History Today and English Heritage 'Beyond 1066'

historiography.summary: Older scholarship treated Orderic Vitalis's '100,000 dead' as broadly credible; recent work (drawing on archaeology and re-reading Domesday's 'waste' entries) sits between catastrophic-genocide claims and a measured-destruction reading. Either way, the political effect — terror that ended large-scale northern revolt — is undisputed.
historiography.source: History Today 'The Harrying of the North'

historiography.summary: Susan Reynolds (Fiefs and Vassals, 1994) argued the 'feudal system' is a 19th-century historians' construct that flattens varied real practices. AQA still teaches feudalism as a working model because students need a framework — but examiners reward students who can describe the real working relationships (military service, land grants, sub-infeudation) rather than chant a textbook hierarchy.
historiography.source: Public scholarship referenced in Oxford and Hodder GCSE textbooks

pedagogy_notes: Order matters: teach Conquest (Part 1) before Control (Part 2) before Society (Part 3) — students need the military narrative pinned down before they can interpret the Domesday landholding pattern or the Church reforms.

Build the historic environment site in across multiple lessons, not just the final lesson. Reference Pevensey when teaching William's landing (Part 1), when teaching castles and patronage (Parts 1-2), and when teaching William II's reign (Part 1). The dedicated site lesson then synthesises rather than introduces.

Use Domesday extracts as a recurring source — short Latin entries with translations work well for 'describe two features' practice and source utility skills, even though source utility is technically a Paper 1 / Paper 2 Section A skill.

Comparative Anglo-Saxon vs Norman framing is required by the spec. Each major topic (government, society, Church, monasticism) needs a 'what was it like before' beat so students can answer 'how far did the Normans change X' questions.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Edward the Confessor
key_individuals_and_groups.role: King of England 1042-1066. His childless death triggered the succession crisis. Likely promised the throne to William in 1051 (Norman claim) but on his deathbed gestured to Harold (English claim).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Harold Godwinson
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Earl of Wessex, then King of England Jan-Oct 1066. Crowned the day after Edward's death. Defeated Hardrada at Stamford Bridge (25 Sep) but was killed at Hastings (14 Oct).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Harald Hardrada
key_individuals_and_groups.role: King of Norway and rival claimant. Invaded the north of England in September 1066 with Tostig Godwinson. Killed at Stamford Bridge.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William the Conqueror (William I)
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Duke of Normandy. Claimed the English throne by promise and oath. Won at Hastings, crowned 25 Dec 1066. Reigned to 1087, dying in Normandy from a riding accident at Mantes.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William II 'Rufus'
key_individuals_and_groups.role: William I's second son, King of England 1087-1100. Faced the 1088 rebellion (with Pevensey at its centre) when Norman barons backed his elder brother Robert Curthose. Killed in the New Forest in a hunting accident, 1100.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert Curthose
key_individuals_and_groups.role: William I's eldest son. Inherited Normandy in 1087 (not England) and led the 1088 rebellion against William Rufus.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert of Mortain
key_individuals_and_groups.role: William I's half-brother. Granted Pevensey Castle and vast lands across England. Backed the 1088 rebellion.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Odo of Bayeux
key_individuals_and_groups.role: William I's other half-brother. Bishop of Bayeux, Earl of Kent. Commissioned the Bayeux Tapestry. Imprisoned 1082; rebelled 1088.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Hereward 'the Wake'
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Lincolnshire thegn who led English resistance from the Isle of Ely, 1070-71. Symbol of Anglo-Saxon defiance; later legend exaggerates his story.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Edgar Atheling
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Anglo-Saxon claimant — grandson of Edmund Ironside. Briefly elected king by the Witan after Hastings before submitting. Centre of multiple revolts.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Lanfranc of Bec
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Italian-born monk, prior at Bec in Normandy. Made Archbishop of Canterbury 1070 by William I. Drove the Norman Church reform — replaced Anglo-Saxon bishops, rebuilt cathedrals, asserted Canterbury primacy over York.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Anselm
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Lanfranc's successor at Bec and at Canterbury (from 1093). Clashed with William II over Church-state authority — early phase of the Investiture Controversy in England.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Stigand
key_individuals_and_groups.role: The Anglo-Saxon Archbishop of Canterbury whom William and the papacy considered illegitimate. Deposed in 1070 to make way for Lanfranc.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Pope Alexander II
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Blessed William's invasion in 1066, sending a papal banner. The Church's pre-conquest endorsement framed the conquest as righteous reform.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Pope Gregory VII
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Drove the wider Investiture Controversy. William I refused to do homage to him for England, setting the pattern for Norman Church-state relations.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Tenants-in-chief

site_dossier.location: Caernarfon, north-west Wales (Gwynedd), at the mouth of the river Seiont where it meets the Menai Strait — strategically chosen at the seat of the former Welsh princes of Gwynedd to project English authority over the conquered heartland.
site_dossier.function: Royal fortress-palace, administrative headquarters and walled borough designed to colonise Gwynedd after Edward's victory in the second Welsh war (1282-83). Combined castle, walled town and quay as a single planned complex.
site_dossier.structure_design: Polygonal towers (not the round towers used at Conwy and Harlech), banded coloured masonry, twin-towered King's Gate facing the town, the Queen's Gate giving access to the river, and the great Eagle Tower with three turrets and walls up to 18 feet thick at the western end. Designed under master military architect Master James of St George, who oversaw the wider Edwardian castle programme.
site_dossier.symbolism: Imperial/Caesarian and Constantinopolitan iconography — banded masonry and angular towers consciously echo the walls of Constantinople and Roman imperial design, cast as a deliberate visual claim that Edward inherited the mantle of Roman emperors who had once campaigned in Britain. The choice of polygonal towers and stone bands set Caernarfon apart from the rest of Edward's Welsh ring.
site_dossier.key_dates: Construction began 1283 immediately after the second Welsh war; royal couple were housed in the Eagle Tower by Easter 1284; Edward of Caernarfon (the future Edward II) born at the castle on 25 April 1284; major damage when Madog ap Llywelyn's revolt sacked the unfinished works in 1294, then repaired and resumed; Edward I's death in 1307 left the castle still incomplete — work continued under Edward II until c.1330, total spend approximately £25,000.
site_dossier.people_connected: Edward I (commissioner and king); Queen Eleanor of Castile (in residence Easter 1284); Edward of Caernarfon (born 25 April 1284, later Edward II, presented as the first English Prince of Wales in 1301); Master James of St George (designer/master of works on the wider Edwardian Welsh castle programme); Sir Otto de Grandison (justice of north Wales); Madog ap Llywelyn (leader of the 1294-95 Welsh revolt that sacked the unfinished works).
site_dossier.links_to_depth_study: Welsh wars (Part 3): the castle was the keystone of Edward's post-1282-83 settlement and its design embodied the Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) administrative shire system. Government and royal authority (Part 1): the planted English borough alongside the castle excluded Welsh inhabitants, asserting royal control through colonisation. Trade and finance (Part 2): the £25,000 build cost drove the wool tax, Italian banker loans (the Riccardi of Lucca then the Frescobaldi) and re-coinage of the late 1270s. Medieval warfare (Part 3): Caernarfon shows the late-thirteenth-century shift from motte-and-bailey to concentric and gatehouse-led design, with arrow loops, machicolations and murder holes designed for siege resistance — proven when the 1294 revolt forced rebuilding.

Royal finance and taxation
Wool tax
Italian bankers
Re-coinage

spec_bullets_covered: Expulsion of the Jews in 1290

Edward's Welsh Wars in 1277 and 1282-83
Statute of Rhuddlan

spec_bullets_covered: Relations with Scotland: 'the Great Cause'
Issue of Scottish succession
Balliol and Bruce
Scottish campaigns

lessons.title: Wallace, Bruce and the 'Hammer of the Scots', 1297-1307
lessons.description: Scottish resistance, the First War of Scottish Independence and Edward's contested legacy.
lessons.spec_part: Part 3 — Edward I's military campaigns in Wales and Scotland
spec_bullets_covered: William Wallace and the First War of Scottish Independence from 1297 to the death of Edward I
The reputation of Edward I as 'Hammer of the Scots'
lessons.lesson_focus: William Wallace's rising 1297 and victory at Stirling Bridge, Edward's victory at Falkirk 1298 and the longbow's emergence as decisive, Wallace's capture and execution 1305, Robert Bruce's coup and coronation as King of Scots February 1306, Edward's death at Burgh-by-Sands on the way north on 7 July 1307, and an evaluation of the 'Hammer of the Scots' tomb-inscription label against the reality of an unfinished conquest.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students often write that the 1295 'Model Parliament' was an elected representative body in the modern sense. In reality every parliament under Edward was summoned by the king for his own purposes — typically to grant taxation or hear judicial business — and the 'commons' element (knights of the shire and burgesses) was widened so the king could raise money more efficiently, not because of a constitutional principle.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B Option B and Pearson/Hodder GCSE History textbooks for the 8145 Edward I option.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students treat the famous 'Hammer of the Scots' label as a contemporary judgement that Edward had crushed Scotland by 1307. The phrase comes from the inscription on Edward's tomb at Westminster (added later, possibly in the sixteenth century) and Edward died on the way to a fresh Scottish campaign with Robert Bruce already crowned and resistance very much alive.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Marc Morris, A Great and Terrible King: Edward I and the Forging of Britain (2008); Westminster Abbey tomb inscription scholarship.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students conflate the two Welsh wars (1277 and 1282-83) with the Scottish wars from 1296 onwards, blurring a fifteen-year gap. Wales is largely settled by the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284; Scottish involvement only begins seriously with the Great Cause of 1290-92.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports flagging chronological confusion across British depth study options.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students frame the expulsion either as a sudden act of personal antisemitism or as purely a financial decision. It was both — a deeply rooted cultural antisemitism reinforced by ritual-murder libels and the 1275 Statute of the Jewry, combined with the political opportunity to extract a parliamentary grant of £116,000 from a grateful tax-paying public in exchange for the edict.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Robin R. Mundill, England's Jewish Solution (1998); History Today scholarship on the 1290 expulsion.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.topic: Edward I, Edward II and Edward III
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students conflate the three Edwards — attributing the loss at Bannockburn (1314, Edward II) or victories of the Hundred Years War (Edward III) to Edward I. The depth study covers only 1272-1307; Bannockburn is seven years after Edward I's death.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B and standard GCSE textbook errata.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students describe Caernarfon as a military fortress only, missing the deliberate triple function of fortress, palace and walled colonial town. The polygonal towers and banded masonry were chosen to broadcast imperial Roman/Constantinopolitan symbolism — its purpose was as much ideological as defensive.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Cadw (Welsh Government heritage agency) Caernarfon Castle official guide and UNESCO World Heritage nomination dossier for the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On the 16-mark historic environment essay, top-band answers explicitly connect features of Caernarfon Castle (e.g. polygonal towers, banded masonry, the planted borough) to wider events of Edward's reign such as the Statute of Rhuddlan, the second Welsh war, the wool tax, or the 1294 Madog revolt — describing the castle in isolation will lose marks.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 for Paper 2 Section B and AQA examiner commentary on historic environment questions.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On 'describe two features' (4 marks), examiners want two clearly separate features each given a supporting detail — students who give one elaborate feature lose half the marks.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B 'describe two features' questions across multiple series.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On 'explain why' / 'explain effects' (8 marks), the highest band requires causal links between events — 'X caused Y because...' — not a parallel list of factors. For Edward I this means treating the Welsh wars, the wool tax, the bankers and the castle programme as a connected system rather than separate topics.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B 8-mark questions.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Students who deploy precise medieval terminology (statute, writ, chancery, exchequer, borough, demesne, bailiff, escheator, eyre, marcher lordship) cluster in higher bands — vague language ('the king made a law') caps marks.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA SPaG performance descriptors (spec section 4.4.3) and examiner reports on candidates' use of specialist vocabulary.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Historiographical awareness — even brief contrast between Marc Morris's view of Edward as a 'great and terrible king' and Michael Prestwich's emphasis on administrative achievement — lifts conclusions on the 16-mark question.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: Marc Morris, A Great and Terrible King (2008) and Michael Prestwich, Edward I (Yale English Monarchs series, rev. 1997); standard A-level transition reading lists.

historiography_notes.view: Edward as efficient administrator and law-giver
historiography_notes.supporting_scholarship: Michael Prestwich's Edward I (Yale English Monarchs, rev. 1997) emphasises the Hundred Rolls inquiry, the Statutes of Westminster (1275, 1285), Gloucester (1278), Mortmain (1279), the Quo Warranto inquiries and the development of parliament as administrative achievements that shaped English government for centuries.

Marc Morris's A Great and Terrible King (2008) and revisionist Welsh and Scottish historians stress the violence of the 1282-83 Welsh war (Llywelyn's killing at Cilmeri, Dafydd's hanging-drawing-and-quartering), the colonial planted boroughs, the 1290 expulsion of the Jews, and the savagery at Berwick in 1296.

Older 'Whig' tradition (Stubbs, Tout) viewed the 1295 Model Parliament as a step towards parliamentary democracy; modern scholarship (David Carpenter, John Maddicott) shows Edward's parliaments were instruments for raising tax and dispensing justice — but the broadened summons did establish a precedent that later kings could not easily reverse.

key_individuals_and_groups: Edward I — king of England 1272-1307, the depth-study protagonist; legal reformer, conqueror of Wales, would-be conqueror of Scotland.
Henry III — Edward's father, whose troubled reign (Provisions of Oxford, Second Barons' War) shaped Edward's determination to restore royal authority.
Eleanor of Castile — Edward's queen, accompanied him on campaign and to Caernarfon for the birth of their heir in 1284; her death in 1290 prompted the Eleanor Crosses.
Robert Burnell — Lord Chancellor 1274-1292, architect of the Hundred Rolls inquiry and the great Edwardian statutes.
Llywelyn ap Gruffudd — Prince of Wales, whose refusal to pay homage triggered the war of 1277 and the war of 1282-83 in which he was killed at Cilmeri.
Dafydd ap Gruffudd — Llywelyn's brother, whose 1282 attack on Hawarden Castle reignited the Welsh war; first nobleman in England executed by hanging, drawing and quartering, 1283.
Master James of St George — Savoyard master of works for Edward's Welsh castle programme; designer (or supervising architect) of Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech and Beaumaris.
Madog ap Llywelyn — leader of the Welsh revolt of 1294-95 that briefly captured Caernarfon's unfinished works.
John Balliol — chosen king of Scots 1292 in the Great Cause; deposed by Edward 1296 after the sack of Berwick.
Robert Bruce (the elder, the Competitor; and his grandson Robert Bruce the future Robert I) — Balliol's rivals in the Great Cause; the younger Bruce would resume the war against Edward I in 1306.
William Wallace — leader of Scottish resistance from 1297; victor at Stirling Bridge 1297, defeated at Falkirk 1298, executed 1305.
Roger Bacon and Duns Scotus — Franciscan scholars symbolising thirteenth-century English learning and the medieval universities (Oxford).
The Italian bankers — the Riccardi of Lucca financed the Welsh wars until 1294; the Frescobaldi of Florence took over royal lending after the Riccardi collapse.
The expelled Jewish community of England — c.2,000-3,000 Jews expelled by royal edict 18 July 1290 after generations of legal discrimination and forced conversion campaigns.

site_2026.location: Richmond-upon-Thames, Surrey, on the south bank of the River Thames
site_2026.confirmed_source: AQA News — GCSE History: Historic environment sites 2026-2028 (aqa.org.uk/news/gcse-history-historic-environment-sites-2026-2028)
site_2026.site_summary: A Jacobean mansion remodelled and lavishly extended in the early 1670s by Elizabeth Murray (Countess of Dysart) and her second husband John Maitland, Duke of Lauderdale, a key member of Charles II's Cabal and Secretary of State for Scotland. Charles II created them Duke and Duchess of Lauderdale and granted Elizabeth a £800 annual pension after the Restoration. The Lauderdales doubled the building southward, installed a suite of rooms intended for Queen Catherine of Braganza, and filled the house with the latest French-influenced fashions, paintings, mirrored cabinets, parterre gardens and household inventories that survive almost untouched.
key_features_to_teach: Location on the Thames between Richmond and Hampton Court — close to the royal court but a private retreat
Function as a Restoration political household: Lauderdale entertained the king's inner circle here while running Scotland
Structure: Jacobean H-plan core (1610) extended south in 1672-74 to create the new state apartments
People connected: Elizabeth Murray, Duchess of Lauderdale; the Duke of Lauderdale; Charles II and Catherine of Braganza as visitors
Design: Long Gallery, Queen's Closet, Cabinet of Miniatures, sleeping arrangements that mirror Versailles court etiquette
How design reflects culture: French baroque taste, Restoration colour and gilding, scagliola, ebony and silver — wealth and proximity to the king as status symbols
Garden: parterre, wilderness and Cherry Garden show the new formal landscape style imported with Charles II from continental exile
Connection to wider events: the Cabal, Lauderdale's hard-line Scottish policy, court intrigue, female agency at the highest political level
links_back_to_period: Court culture and royal favour as the engine of social mobility (Part 1: Charles II's court; Part 2: court fashions)
The Cabal and patronage politics of the early 1670s (Part 1: Crown and Parliament)
Restoration architecture, design and decorative arts (Part 2: architecture and design, Wren parallel)
Status and influence of women in Restoration society (Part 2: role and status of women)
Wealth flowing from trade, slavery and overseas land grants into elite consumption (Part 3: trade, mercantilism)

lessons.title: The Road Back to the Throne: Restoration of the Monarchy 1660
lessons.description: Why Charles II was invited home — the legacy of Civil War and Commonwealth and the Declaration of Breda settlement.
spec_bullets_covered: Crown and Parliament: the legacy of the English Civil War and Commonwealth; the restoration of the monarchy
key_content: Death of Cromwell 1658 and collapse of the Protectorate under Richard Cromwell
General Monck's march south and the Convention Parliament of 1660
Declaration of Breda: indemnity, religious toleration, arrears of army pay, parliamentary settlement
Charles II's entry into London 29 May 1660 — public mood and limits of triumph
Act of Indemnity and Oblivion 1660 — regicides excluded, the body of Cromwell exhumed and hanged
What was actually restored: monarchy, House of Lords, Anglican Church; abolished prerogative courts and feudal tenures stayed gone
lessons.exam_focus: Effects of the Restoration settlement on government and the army

lessons.title: The Cavalier Parliament and the Religious Settlement
lessons.description: How the Cavalier Parliament locked Anglicanism back into law and which groups it pushed to the margins.
spec_bullets_covered: relations and issues with Parliament, finance and religion
key_content: Election of the Cavalier Parliament 1661 — overwhelmingly royalist and Anglican
The four laws known as the Clarendon Code: Corporation Act 1661, Act of Uniformity 1662, Conventicle Act 1664, Five Mile Act 1665
Great Ejection 1662: around 2,000 ministers expelled from the Church of England
Definition and treatment of Dissenters/Nonconformists — Quakers, Baptists, Presbyterians, Independents
Charles II's preference for toleration vs Parliament's hard line — the 1672 Declaration of Indulgence withdrawn 1673
Royal finance: customs, hearth tax, the chronic gap between income and need
lessons.exam_focus: Two features of the Clarendon Code

lessons.title: The Cabal, Party Politics and Rule Without Parliament
lessons.description: How Charles II governed in the 1670s — through a five-man inner circle, then alone after 1681.
spec_bullets_covered: the Cabal and 'Party politics'; rule without parliament from 1681
key_content: Fall of Clarendon 1667 after the Second Dutch War
The Cabal ministry: Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley (later Shaftesbury), Lauderdale — what each contributed
Secret Treaty of Dover 1670: French subsidy, conversion clause, war on the Dutch
Test Act 1673 forces Catholics out of office — Clifford and James, Duke of York resign
Emergence of Court (Tory) and Country (Whig) factions during the Exclusion Crisis
Oxford Parliament 1681 dissolved after one week — Charles rules without Parliament 1681-85, financed by a new French subsidy
lessons.exam_focus: Effects of the Cabal on Charles II's government

lessons.title: Charles II: The King and His Court
lessons.description: Charles II's character, his court, royal mistresses and what 'court life' actually meant in the 1660s and 1670s.
spec_bullets_covered: Charles II's court: Charles II's character; court life, fashions and the role of the court
key_content: Charles II's character: charming, clever, cynical; lessons of exile in France and the Low Countries
The court at Whitehall — over 2,000 rooms, 1,000 staff, public and private spheres
Royal mistresses as political actors: Barbara Villiers (Castlemaine), Nell Gwyn, Louise de Kéroualle
Catherine of Braganza, Portuguese Catholic queen, childless — the seed of the succession crisis
French fashions: long wigs, vests (1666), heeled shoes, formal dance, Italian opera
Court culture as politics: who got near the king got patronage and place
lessons.exam_focus: Significance of court life for politics and culture

lessons.title: The Great Plague of 1665
lessons.description: Causes, contemporary explanations, official measures and consequences of London's last great plague.
spec_bullets_covered: Crisis: Great Plague of 1665; causes and contemporary views; measures to combat; records; results
key_content: Outbreak in St Giles spring 1665, peak August-September with 7,000+ weekly deaths
Bills of Mortality and parish records — what they show and what they hide
Contemporary causes: miasma, sin, the comet of 1664, conjunctions of planets — almost no germ theory
Measures: shutting up infected houses with red cross and 'Lord have mercy upon us', plague pits, killing dogs and cats, fires in streets, court flees to Oxford
Total deaths around 100,000 — perhaps a fifth of London's population
Pepys's Diary: a privileged eyewitness who stayed for work and commuted from Greenwich
lessons.exam_focus: The events of the Great Plague of 1665

lessons.title: The Great Fire of London 1666: Disaster and Reconstruction
lessons.description: How a bakery fire became a city-destroying inferno and what rose from the ashes under Wren.
spec_bullets_covered: Fire of London of 1666; causes and contemporary views; results and reconstruction
key_content: 2-6 September 1666: Pudding Lane bakery, Lord Mayor Bloodworth's fatal indecision, easterly winds, timber and pitch
Charles II and James, Duke of York take personal command of firefighting — gunpowder and demolition
Scale of destruction: 13,200 houses, 87 churches, St Paul's, the Royal Exchange, the Guildhall — four-fifths of the City
Contemporary views: arson by Catholics or Dutch — Robert Hubert hanged after a false confession; the Monument inscription
Rebuilding Acts 1667 and 1670: brick and stone, wider streets, regulated trades, but Wren's grand street plan rejected
Wren's 51 City churches and St Paul's Cathedral 1675-1710 — money from a coal tax
lessons.exam_focus: Whether the Fire's effects were more positive than negative for London

lessons.title: The Catholic Question: Popish Plot and Rye House Plot
lessons.description: How Titus Oates's lies and a real assassination plan brought England to the edge of revolution.
spec_bullets_covered: The Catholic question: plots, including Titus Oates and the Popish Plot and the Rye House Plot
key_content: Background: anti-Catholicism, fear of France, James's open Catholicism after 1673
Titus Oates and Israel Tonge fabricate the Popish Plot autumn 1678 — claim Jesuits will assassinate Charles
Murder of Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey October 1678 — magistrate who took Oates's deposition
Around 35 Catholics executed; mass hysteria sweeps the country
Rye House Plot 1683: real Whig conspiracy to ambush and kill Charles and James — Russell and Sidney executed
Aftermath: a Tory reaction, purge of corporations, Charles's authority restored
lessons.exam_focus: Events of the Popish Plot 1678-81

lessons.title: The Exclusion Crisis and the Succession
lessons.description: Three Parliaments, three Exclusion Bills and the birth of Whigs and Tories — could a Catholic king be stopped?
spec_bullets_covered: the Exclusion Bill, 1679; James, Duke of York; the succession issue
key_content: James, Duke of York: open Catholic from 1673, heir presumptive to a childless king
Three Exclusion Bills 1679, 1680, 1681 — would have barred James from the throne
Shaftesbury and the Whigs argue parliamentary right to determine succession
Tories defend hereditary right and the Anglican settlement
Charles dissolves the Oxford Parliament March 1681 — turning point
Monmouth (Charles's illegitimate Protestant son) as alternative heir — sidelined; later rebels in 1685
lessons.exam_focus: Whether the Exclusion Crisis was mainly about religion or about power

lessons.title: Restoration Stage, Coffee Houses and Women in Public Life
lessons.description: Theatres reopen, women perform on stage for the first time, and coffee houses become the engine of public news.
spec_bullets_covered: Restoration culture: Restoration comedy, theatres and playwrights; the role and status of women; coffee houses
key_content: 1660 patents to Killigrew (King's Company) and Davenant (Duke's Company) — only two licensed theatres in London
Women on stage from 1660-61: actresses including Nell Gwyn, Elizabeth Barry — replacing boys in female roles
Restoration comedy: Etherege, Wycherley, Congreve, Behn — wit, sex, social satire; the shock of female playwrights
Aphra Behn — first English woman to make a living from writing
Coffee houses from 1652 (London's first) — penny universities, news, business, political gossip; Charles II's failed ban 1675
Wider role and status of women: still under coverture in law but visible at court, on stage, in print

lessons.title: The Royal Society, Pepys and the New Science
lessons.description: How a group of London gentlemen built the world's leading scientific society under Charles II's patronage.
spec_bullets_covered: Charles II's patronage of the arts and sciences, including the Royal Society; Samuel Pepys; architecture and design, including Christopher Wren
key_content: First meeting Gresham College November 1660 after a lecture by Christopher Wren
Royal Charter 1662, second charter 1663 — 'Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge'
A private subscription society — fellows paid their own dues; no Treasury funding
Key figures: Wilkins, Boyle, Hooke, Wren, later Newton (President from 1703)
Pepys: fellow from 1665, President 1684-86, signs the imprimatur of Newton's Principia 1687
Wren beyond St Paul's: the Royal Observatory at Greenwich (founded 1675), Royal Hospital Chelsea, Trinity College Library Cambridge
lessons.exam_focus: Significance of royal patronage for the new science

lessons.title: Sea Power, the Navigation Acts and the Dutch Wars
lessons.description: How England fought three wars with the Dutch to control trade — and what mercantilism meant in practice.
spec_bullets_covered: Trade: mercantilism; the Navigation Acts and their impact
War: English sea power; naval warfare, including tactics and technology; conflict with the Dutch, including the Second and Third Dutch Wars; relations with Spain and France
key_content: Mercantilism: zero-sum view of trade; bullion, colonies, monopoly companies
Navigation Acts 1660, 1662, 1663 — only English/colonial ships in colonial trade; goods landed in England first
Second Dutch War 1665-67: early English success at Lowestoft; humiliation at the Medway 1667 when De Ruyter burned the fleet at Chatham
Treaty of Breda 1667 — England keeps New York, Dutch keep Suriname
Third Dutch War 1672-74: alongside France under the Treaty of Dover; ended early when Parliament forced peace
Naval technology: line-of-battle tactics, the three-deck ship of the line, Pepys's reforms of victualling and shipbuilding
lessons.exam_focus: Effects of the Navigation Acts on English trade and shipping

lessons.title: Empire, Slavery and the End of the Reign 1685
lessons.description: Bombay, Tangier, Hudson Bay and Jamaica — how England's overseas reach grew, on whose backs, and where the reign left the country.
spec_bullets_covered: Land: the powers of the East India Company; Bombay; Hudson Bay; Tangier; Captain Henry Morgan and Jamaica
Trade: slave trade
key_content: Catherine of Braganza's dowry 1662: Bombay (Mumbai) and Tangier
East India Company: chartered 1600, given Bombay 1668, granted near-sovereign powers — fortifications, mint, justice
Hudson's Bay Company chartered 1670 — fur trade, English claim to North America
Jamaica seized 1655 (Cromwell), kept at Restoration; sugar, slavery, and Henry Morgan's privateering — Panama 1671

teaching_brief.overall_narrative_arc: The unit moves from celebration to crisis to consolidation. It opens with the political settlement of 1660 and asks what the Restoration actually restored. It then walks through the religious code that excluded Dissenters, the foreign and domestic shocks of Plague, Fire and the Dutch wars, and the way succession anxiety boiled into the Popish Plot and Exclusion Crisis. From there students study the rich social and cultural world the same regime nurtured — theatre, science, coffee houses, building — and then follow English power overseas through the Navigation Acts, Bombay, Jamaica and the slave trade. The historic environment lesson uses Ham House to make the period tangible. The unit closes by judging Charles II's reign in the round so students can write substantiated 16-mark essays.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume 1660 was a return to absolute monarchy and that the Civil War was 'forgotten'. In fact Parliament emerged stronger, taxation became a negotiated relationship, and unresolved tensions over religion and succession would explode in the Exclusion Crisis and 1688.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B Option D Restoration England; Tim Harris, Restoration: Charles II and his Kingdoms

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse 1665 (Plague) and 1666 (Fire) and assume one caused or cured the other. The plague was waning before the Fire began on 2 September 1666; the Fire did not 'burn out' the plague.
common_misconceptions.source: Royal Museums Greenwich, The Great Plague and The Great Fire of London; Museum of London Great Plague resources

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students think the Royal Society was a government department funded by the Crown. It was a private subscription society of gentlemen-amateurs that received a royal charter (1662) and royal interest, but no Treasury money — fellows paid their own way.
common_misconceptions.source: Royal Society 'History of the Royal Society'; History Today, The Royal Society's First Charter

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students over-romanticise the Restoration as a carefree party after Puritan austerity. Court culture was politically charged: mistresses had French diplomatic links, theatre was censored, and religious and party tensions ran underneath the wit.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA mark schemes for Paper 2B/D on Charles II's character and court; Royal Museums Greenwich, The Restoration

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume modern political parties existed throughout the period. Whig and Tory labels only emerge during the Exclusion Crisis (1679-81) as nicknames; they were factions, not parties, and most MPs sat without a label.
common_misconceptions.source: Tim Harris, Restoration revisionist scholarship; UK Parliament living-heritage 1660-1688 timeline

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students think Clarendon wrote it. The four laws (Corporation Act, Act of Uniformity, Conventicle Act, Five Mile Act) were driven by the Cavalier Parliament, not Clarendon, who actually favoured wider toleration.
common_misconceptions.source: UK Parliament, Act of Uniformity 1662 and 1660-1688 key dates; AQA mark scheme commentary on the religious settlement

Top-band answers use site features as evidence for an argument about court politics, design, women's status or patronage.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA mark scheme for 8145/2B/D, June 2023 onwards

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Explain Effects (8 marks) wants consequences, not narrative. Top answers build chains: event -> effect on group -> wider effect on society/politics, with at least two distinct effects developed.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B Option D

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Significance questions reward importance both at the time and over time. For Restoration topics this often means tracing a 1660s event forward to 1688 or beyond.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports; spec section 4.4.2 Significance descriptors

historiography_notes: Tim Harris's revisionist work (Restoration, 2005; Revolution, 2006) reframes Charles II as a politically skilful king navigating real party formation rather than a 'merry monarch'.
Lisa Jardine on Wren and the rebuilding of London situates St Paul's and the City churches as scientific as well as architectural achievements.
Claire Tomalin on Pepys foregrounds the Diary as social history not just naval administration.
Use historiography sparingly — only where it sharpens an exam-relevant argument.
